Mr. Chairman, the Solicitor General is not quite correct in stating that this measure was introduced by me last year. In the first session of 1919, that which immediately followed the cessation of hostilities, I proposed the following resolution, which appears as No. 37 on page 25 of the Order Paper of Monday, April 7:
That, in the opinion of this House, November 11 of each year should be set aside as a day of national thanksgiving', to be a perpetual memorial to the signing of the armistice, ending the great world war.
Almost immediately after that resolution appeared on the Order Paper the press of Canada from one end of the country to the other commented favourably on the proposal. But for some years prior to that time, at the request of the Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada, Thanksgiving Day had been observed on the Monday of the week in which that holiday ordinarily occurred. A delegation of commercial travellers came from Toronto to Ottawa, bringing with them the secretary of their association, and interviewed me with a view towards seeing whether I would not adopt as the holiday the day on which the armistice was signed, which was the second Monday in November, instead of adopting the date, November 11. In my judgment it mattered very little

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
whether the exact date or the exact day was named; either would serve the idea I had in mind, and th'e naming of the day instead of the date would, at the same time, meet the wishes of this large and influential body of citizens. In view, therefore, of the representations then made I had no hesitation in adopting the suggestion, and instead of proceeding with my resolution as it appeared on the Order Paper I introduced, on April 9, 1919, Bill No. 66, "An Act respecting Thanksgiving Day." This Bill was prepared by the parliamentary counsel, so I presume it was in proper form. The Bill was as follows:
1. The annual thanksgiving day, heretofore held on a day fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council, shall hereafter be held on the second Monday of November in each year, as a perpetual memorial of the victorious conclusion of the recent war, in addition to such other reasons as may be prescribed by proclamation of the Governor in Council for that purpose published; and paragraph (11) of section thirty-four of the Interpretation Act, and paragraph (a) of section forty-three of the Bills of Exchange Act, chapters one, and one hundred and nineteen, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, are amended by adding "Thanksgiving Day" to the lists of holidays and non-juridical days, mentioned in the said paragraphs.
This Bill received its ,first reading in the first session of 1919. I endeavoured to have it proceeded with during that session but without success. However, during the second session of 1919, on September 4, I introduced a Bill in exactly the same form, Bill No. 2.
I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that clause 2 of the Bill is under consideration. I am afraid he is wandering away from that clause.

I am keeping as close as I can to clause 2. I wish to give the reasons for an amendment which I intend to propose, and my remarks are all leading up to that point. Shall I proceed, Mr. Chairman, along that line?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would reach the conclusion without laying the foundation.

It is necessary that I should proceed in this way, because the Solicitor General, who has charge of this Bill, has stated that it was introduced at the last session, which is not correct, and I want to show the history of the Bill. Now, Bill No. 2 was passed through several stages in the second session of 1919 and was brought down to the third reading.

On the third reading a difficulty arose through the fact that the Bill had been amended in committee and it was my desire that it should be again referred back for consideration. The member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) on that occasion, moved the six months' hoist, and the motion was carried by the small majority of five. I felt then, as I feel to-day, that the Bill as originally! introduced by me had (many features of merit and was deserving of better consideration at the hands of the House. I felt, and still feel, that the opposition to the Bill was not in accordance with the best traditions of this House. It seemed to be the determination of hon. gentlemen opposite that because this Bill had been introduced by a member of the Opposition, it should be thrown out. In that connection I should not include all hon. gentlemen opposite, because I noted with pleasure that several leading members and supporters of the Government approved of and voted for the measure as introduced by me at that time. It was a great pleasure to me to have had that support, but on that occasion there was, on the Goverivment side of the House, a certain circle of members who seemed to be seized of the idea that it was an intolerable situation for a member of the Opposition to get away with a proposition of this kind. Consequently, the order went forth that the Bill must be killed in the final stages, so the executioner came along and the hon. member for Perth South was the chief executioner on that occasion.
To administer poison.

It was not a slow poison, I can assure the committee, because it was sudden death on that occasion. From that time to the present, there have been appeals from one end of the country to the other for reconsideration of this matter, and last Armistice Day the appeal was so insistent that it evidently had its effect. I am sorry that Canada was denied by a small majority of -her representatives the privilege of observing Armistice Day on the first anniversary of that event and of continuing the observance for all time to come. Armistice Day appealed to me, not for the purpose of observing a great victory over our enemies, but for the purpose of observing a cessation of the hostilities that had raged so long in the great world war. To-day I do not see any reason why the change suggested by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) in the first instance this year, and the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), who

has taken over the measure on behalf of the Government to see it through on the present occasion should be made. I understand, in a general way, that the change is made out of regard for the feelings of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt), who was one of the strenuous opponents of my proposition in the first instance. I do not see any reason why the proposition as introduced by me in the first instance should be changed now. The change does not add to clearness in the matter, and, as a matter of fact, it makes the proposition so indefinite and roundabout that one would have to do some figuring before he could reach a definite conclusion which day was intended to be observed. If you, Sir, will follow me in reading the second clause of the Bill, I think you will come to the same conclusion. I think you are clear enough in vision and intelligence to do so. The clause reads:
Throughout Canada in each and every year the Monday in the week to which is the eleventh day of November, being the day in 1918 in which the Great War was triumphantly concluded by an armistice by which Canada was delivered from her enemies, shall be a legal holiday and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of Armistice Day.
That phraseology reminds me of the Irishman's clock, one of those old wag-of-the-wall on which you pull a chain in order to wind it up. Some of the older members of the House may have seen an instrument of that kind. By the way, the clocks around this chamber remind me somewhat of the incident to which I am referring, because no two of them are ever at the same time.
They are on opposite sides.

The priest made one of his usual calls at the house of this countryman of mine, and he looked up at the clock and he said to Pat: "How do you tell the time of day by your clock? It does not seem to be in harmony with the correct time." Pat replied: "Your reverence, that's aisy; when the hands point to a quarter past two, then she strikes nine, then I know it is half past six." That is about the position of affairs in this Bill. When the eleventh day of November appears in the week, then it is quite easy to figure out when Armistice Day will occur, if you know how.
My proposition-to get down to brass tacks-as the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Gordon) suggests, is this. I beg to move that clause 2 be further amended in the following way; that
all the words between the word "year" in the fifth line and the word "being" in the seventh line be struck out, and the following be inserted instead: "On the second Monday in November," so that the clause will read:	-
Throughout Canada in each and every year on the second Monday in November, being the day in 1918 in which the Great War was triumphantly concluded by an armistice by which Canada was delivered from her enemies, shall be a legal holiday and shall Ibe kept and observed as such under the name of Armistice Day.
I sincerely trust the acting Solicitor General and others supporting him on the Government side of the House will see the reasonableness of this proposition. It will make this Bill so much more clear and definite, and it will name the day on which armistice was signed. The Bill as drafted names neither the exact day nor 4 p.m. the exact date. In my judgment, it would be in the interest of the country in general if my proposition was accepted and the Bill as originally drafted and presented to this House in 1919 were accepted by the Government. I do not see that they have anything to lose in accepting my proposition now, and I am sure the country will approve my suggestion because it will make the definite day on which the armistice was signed the day of observance for all time to come. The proposition as embodied in the Bill before the committee does not do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Might I suggest that, perhaps, the purpose which my hon. friend has in mind in making a little more clear the particular Monday in November for taking the holiday, would be met if his amendment were accepted by the committee, with the insertion after the words "being the day," of the words "of the week in that month."
The clause would then read:
Throughout Canada in each and every year on-the second Monday in November, being the day of the week in that month in 1918, in which the great war was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a legal holiday.
And so forth. It is just a matter of words, but I think this wording is better.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the words in the clause are miuch more clear than the words read by my ,hon. friend. This year the second Monday falls on the 14th, and that is considered too late in parts of the Dominion of Canada to hold Thanksgiving Day.

I would accept the
amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and in answer to the Acting Solictor General, I beg to inform the committee that the difference in time is so trifling that it is not worth arguing over. Uuder the proposition as suggested by the Solicitor General the earliest that the holiday can be is the 6th of the month, and the latest is the 12th. Under the proposition as I have made it-and for the sake of clearness and directness I appeal to hon. members to accept it-the earliest it can occur is the 8th and the latest is the 14th. The main reason for the difference being made is that the Government will not accept the proposition from the Opposition, and I think it is an unworthy one.

I do not want to prolong the debate, but I would say the earlier the date, the better. Most sportsmen in Ontario are off hunting the first couple of weeks in November, and they want a holiday when the weather is good. Also for a holiday during which there can be any movement of troops, the earlier the date the better; so much so, that for years in view of the fall manoeuvres in Ontario, Thanksgiving was shifted on to the middle of October. I think the amendment is shifting the date too far back. I would rather have the Government date than a week later.

My hon. friend scarcely understands my point. The difference is only two days at the most. The latest it will be held, under the Bill as introduced, is the 12th of November, and, under the amendment, the 14th; the earliest it will be held, under the Bill, is the 6th, and the earliest, under the amendment, the 8th. There is only a difference of two days in either case.
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
The Air Board-salaries, $75,000; contingencies, $25,000; Civil Aviation, $700,000; Canadian Air Force, $825,000.
Just what is this for?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
As the committee is
aware, an Air Board was established by legislation in this country in the spring,

I think, of 1920. Last year was practically the first year of our operations, and was largely taken up with the work of organization and of getting ready. The amount expended last year was considerably in excess of the amount asked for this year, by something like $375,000. There are two branches of the Air Service, the Civil Aviation Branch, and the Canadian Air Force, which is an adjunct to the military service of Canada. The four items which appear in this Estimate fairly represent the work of the Board and the expenditure of the money. Our salary list amounts to about $75,000, and we have 106 employees.
What is meant by "Civil Aviation?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It is work in connection with civil flying, purely and simply. We are attempting to do, in fact last year we accomplished, considerable work in what might be called research or exploration. The board has established provincial boards throughout the Dominion, the presiding officer of these provincial boards being the Lieutenant Governor of the province. The provincial board meets periodically, discusses the situation in regard to its own province, and makes recommendations to the Government. Several of the provinces have agreed with the Air Board to stand half the expense of all flying operations undertaken within their territory. We have such an agreement with the province of British Columbia, with Alberta, and, I think, although I am not sure,-I could ascertain the fact readily -with the province of Ontario. The Board did a lot of valuable work last year in the province of Quebec. It surveyed all the northern part of Quebec from Lake St. John for a distance of 250 miles north, and I believe that the results obtained in two weeks, flying operations were far better than the work accomplished during five years of progress on the land. Air photographs have been taken of all that territory, showing the location of the lakes, the rivers, and the timber areas, the photographs being distinct enough to show the burnt timber and to distinguish hard wood from soft wood; in most cases also, it shows whether streams are navigable or not. These photographs were regarded as a great achievement by the Air Force, and were welcomed by the province of Quebec. In British Columbia, we do fire ranging, and some exploration work on the coast, and we are also establishing a station there in connection with timber in the railroad

belt. As the House is aware, the Dominion of Canada owns a very valuable block of timber in the heart of British Columbia. In Alberta, something is being done in the exploration of the northern territory; the work there has not been as far advanced as it has been in the province of Ontario. It is hoped that during the coming season the Air Service will be of the greatest assistance in connection with the surveys of oil lands, etc. They are making preparations now in that respect, although actual work has not yet been begun. Work is also being carried on in connection with fire ranging in the Rocky mountains. This is all a part of the work of the Civil Aviation Branch, fn addition, an air line has been mapped out across the continent, and certain landing stations have been erected. But the policy has not been to establish such stations at the expense of the Dominion; the municipalities desiring landing stations must establish them; the Board locates them and leaves it to the municipalities to decide whether they want landing stations established at these places. As the committee is aware, we received a very large number of aircraft from the British Government at the conclusion of the war. We have not been required to purchase much in the' line of aircraft equipment, although year after year our equipment will become more and more obsolete. New inventions are taking place almost monthly, and certainly quarterly. Great improvements were made last year over the year before, and I anticipate that as time goes on there will have to be an appropriation for new aircraft. The figures to-day, however, do not contemplate such an appropriation. We are practically operating now with machines given us.
How many airships are in commission in the two services, respectively, and how many men are employed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not know that I can give the number of machines that we have at present; there are a large number of them not actually in operation, not having yet been fitted up for the purpose. The following machines have been erected and tested: 12 D.H. 9A's.-These are technical terms-12 S.E. 5 A's; 43 Avlo, 135 h.p.; and 6 D.H. 4. We have 105 civil employees, and we have taken over Camp Borden, which is our military air centre, and fitted it up as an aviation station. We have there an air superintendent, a superintendent of engine repair shops-
What are their salaries?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The following is a list of these employees:
Air Foreman Mechanic	 2,040
Superintendent of Engine Repair Shops. 2,940
Air Pilot and Navigator	 2,460
Air Foreman Meeanic	 2,040
Air Foreman Mechanics (3) each.. ..	1,800
Four Air Riggers	at	1,620Nine Air Riggers	at	1,320Five Engine Fitters	at	1,620Ten Air Engine Fitters	at	1,320One Air Fabric Worker	at	1,080Two Carpenters	at	1,080One Motor Transport Driver	at	1,080One Sign Painter	at	1,080Two Clerk-Stenographers	at	960
Is that in the civil force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That is all in the
military force.
Have you the civil force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The civil force totals 105. In the operations branch we have 16; in the certificates branch, 6; headquarters, Canadian Air Service, 7; secretary's office, 2; technical branch, 5; equipment branch, 17; medical branch, 2; accounts branch, 27; intelligence branch, 8; records branch, 15.
What is the reason for the increase of 50 per cent in salaries over last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The chief increase is due to increase in staff. These salaries are fixed by the Civil Service Commission, under whom all appointments are made. In connection with the mechanics, it must be remembered that there are at Camp Borden a large number of expert men. In one or two instances we could not get any men in Canada; we had to bring them from Great Britain. These are the highest type of artisans, and as a rule they call for more than the ordinary artisan's salary. They are expert and highly trained men.
Mr. EULER [DOT] Is there any system of allocating the civil aviation force to the various provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is done in accordance with the demands made upon us.
By whom?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
By the provincial associations, with the concurrence of the Provincial Governments, because, unless the Provincial Government is prepared to stand part of the expense, we do not undertake the work. We have done some work, however, wholly at the expense of the Dominion Government, in Alberta, and, I think, in

British Columbia. The provinces send in their recommendations and we allocate the work according as the staff is available, and as we have the money. The demands on us for the coming season are perhaps a little more than as represented in this vote. I have the particulars and the matter may come to the House on another vote; but I cannot speak with certainty in that regard because it is not settled.
Do the Provincial Governments contribute anything to the air force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, for civil aviation in connection with work done for the provinces in the way of exploration, surveys, fire protection, etc. They enter into an agreement on a fifty-fifty basis.

'Is it the intention to continue the civil air force? When did the Government decide to undertake the work of surveying the different provinces? Is not that work that should be done by the provinces themselves, and not by the Dominion?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This work is not being done for the provinces alone. There are territories of our own, belonging to Canada and not to any province, away to the North, and also in the Railway Belt, in which we operate. Work has also been performed in connection with our coast service. I suppose as time goes on the usefulness of the airship will be demonstrated. Only a few days ago we were asked to act for the Government of the Dominion in connection with customs examinations at Victoria [DOT]and Vancouver, and if the money is voted by Parliament we will certainly do so. It Is charged that there has been a good deal of smuggling of drugs, opium and the like, into Vancouver and Victoria, these drugs being dropped from incoming ships into the ocean and picked up by small vessels; and air craft can be very readily and satisfactorily used not only in the detection of such operations but also in their prevention. We have experimented in that direction and, since our airships have taken part in the work of prevention, that class of smuggling has largely ceased. Then there is work, and a great deal of work, asked of us in regard to Dominion lands by the Department of the Interior. As the House is aware these lands are largely vacant lands and in regard to them a very long programme has been prepared-at least it is now in the shape of requisitions which have not yet been finally passed upon.

My hon. friend says the airship will prove its worth in the years to come. I do not know if my hon. friend has reference to a special class of airships but, as a matter of fact, I thought the success of that invention was proven beyond a shadow of doubt. I happened to be in Europe a year or so ago and every evening after seven I would go from my hotel to the Place de l'Opera in order to get the London Times which came every day by airship and was delivered in Paris in a few hours. During the Versailles conference I saw that Mr. Bonar Law would not travel otherwise than by airship between London and Paris. I suppose that before long the mails will be transported by airship. Has , the experiment not been tried in the United States and was it not successful? I thought it was.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is no question as to its being successful as a system of transportation but it is practically prohibitive up to the present time on account of the cost. That is the difficulty in the matter of air craft operating between London and Paris; I made inquiries last October in regard to that service. Not only do they carry newspapers and mails, but banks utilize them for the carriage of their more valuable parcels, considering it a more secure method for transporting valuable parcels containing'money, jewellery and the like, than the ordinary mail service. But notwithstanding that, the experience of the service up to the present time is that it has not been made a commercial success. Neither has it been made a commercial success by any line operating in the United States. There is a theory- so far only a theory, I believe-that the airship itself will never be a commercial success.
But the word "never" is not in your dictionary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It will be a most valuable adjunct in naval and military matters and the like. But when we come down to the question of commercial success we will be thrown back on the lighter-than-air craft, not on the airship. The lighter-than-air craft, of course, carries nothing for its own support, while the airship has not only to do that but carry its gasoline for propulsion which attaches so much weight that it cannot take on very much cargo. It may be in time-that is the possibility anyway-that the, lighter-than-air craft, not on the airship. That is the hope, and that is the contention

of people who are building such air craft to-day; but I do not think that either kind of craft has yet proved to be commercially successful.

This resolution is one of the explanations why the national debt of this country Jias increased one hundred millions during last year. No doubt it is a nice thing to be able to experiment with airships, no doubt they can be put to useful purposes, but it is a question, can we afford it? I say we can't. The minister says that he has got these airships from the Old Country for nothing, but we have all heard of the tale of the young people who were setting up in life and who were ruined by having a fine parlour clock. At first they had to furnish their parlour to go with the clock, and then they had to furnish their dining room to harmonize with the parlour, and so on with the rest of the House. I suppose it is an ungracious thing to look an airship in the wing or a gift ship in the prow, but I wish to protest against this expenditure. I suppose it will be futile, the Government will pass this resolution. But I do protest most energetically on behalf of the tax-laden people -the long-suffering electors of this country-against this waste of money. Perhaps it is not an absolute waste, there will be some good obtained out of it, but we cannot afford it. The country cannot afford this experimenting with civil aviation. I noticed a few days ago, and I think the minister has just referred to it, that they had to' stop the operation of a commercial line of airships between London and Paris. Well, if two of the wealthiest nations in the world, only situated a comparatively short distance apart, cannot find enough traffic to make their airships pay then it is an act of madness-* and I speak with all respect to those identified with it,-to be going on in this way. We should not spend this amount of money. Of course, as far as the military airships are concerned I would not be opposed to some reasonable expenditure upon them, because if we are to have any military expenditure whatsoever, aviation is one of the branches which has to be maintained; but this civil aviation and this most unsound and unwholesome principle of dividing expenses with the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis, merits criticism. One of the things the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) drank in as a law student was that divided ownerships is a fruitful cause of litigation. Divided control is of the same nature, and we are having far too
much of it in this country. We are having too much of this dividing of control with the provinces on this, that and the other thing. The provinces should pay for their own fire protection and we should not contribute to it-we are sufficiently heavily laden and we should simply represent the people of the Dominion as a whole. I do not think there is any use, the House being constituted as it is, in taking up time by insisting upon a division, but I do wish to register emphatic, and I trust well-founded, protest against this vote. It should be cut in half or cut down by two-thirds at least.
Can the minister tell us, in connection with the item of $850,000 expended last year, what part was contributed by the provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not know that I could give more than an estimate. I would think between $35,000 and $40,000 for four provinces.
It is a very large proportion.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That represents the
whole cost. The work undertaken for the provinces is paid on a fifty-fifty basis, but the civil item under discussion represents far more than the work undertaken for the provinces. It represents all the work undertaken for the Dominion of Canada. I have a synopsis of the work performed, and if it is deemed to be of interest I shall give it.

Let us have the synopsis.
Mr. Guthrie : Speaking of the province of Quebec it says:
This operation was undertaken at the request of the province of Quebec.
It was established at Roberval, Quebec.
It was established as an experiment to show the value of air craft in forest patrol and survey and to facilitate the exploration of the forest areas north and west of Lake St.' John.
The Forestry officers of the Quebec Government have shown the keenest interest in the experiment, and their co-operation has ensured its success.
The free use of a suitable site on the shores of Lake St. John, at Roberval, was given by the courtesy of Lt.-Col. J. A. Scott, of Quebec. Buildings and a slipway were erected by the provincial Government. Two H.S. 2L. machines were flown from Halifax to the station, arriving on July 19th. Flying continued uninterruptedly until the end of October, when winter put an end to the work of the season. The work was carried out under the direction of the Provincial Department of Lands and Forests. Many reconnaissance trips were made; caches were established to allow of patrols being

pushed further afield in future; and photographic surveys were made of the main river-courses in the district.
The provincial authorities have expressed themselves as being fully satisfied with the results of the experiment and have asked for its continuance and extension next season. They are prepared to increase their expenditure on the work considerably, and wish the patrol extended to Lake Mistassini and, if possible, to the shores of James Bay. The total flying time from the station was 73 hours. No accident to personnel or machines occurred.
Operational cost to date, $17,344.34.
That is the Dominion share of the operating cost on that survey. We also have a station at Halifax:
The Naval air stations established during the war at Halifax and North Sydney by the Department of the Naval Service were transferred to the Air Board during 1920 with all aircraft, equipment and material on the stations. As the expense ot maintaining two stations on the Atlantic coast was not justified, it was decided that the base at North Sydney should be closed, and that the material there should be transferred to Halifax or other stations, where it was required for immediate use. This work was completed during the summer.
Halifax station has been maintained as an Operations Branch station for the erection and repair of seaplanes. As this station is open all the year round, it provided an' ideal location for this purpose. Air-routes suitable for water-type machines lead to all parts of eastern and central Canada. The machines required for operations as far west as Winnipeg can be flown from Halifax in the spring, and back to their base in the fall, for overhaul and repair, before ice forms in these districts. This station also provides a base for combined training with the Naval Service and the local garrison.
Constructional cost to date	?	157 90
Operational cost to date	 49,248 67
Then we have a station at Morley, Alberta :
The main purpose served by this station is the. provision of better fire protection in the Dominion Government Forest Reserve on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, from the International Boundary north to the Yellow-head Pass. The havoc caused by forest fires has been very great, and if better control can be obtained from the air, the expense of the operations will be amply justified. The Forestry Branch of the Department of the Interior are keenly interested in the work and have given the closest co-operation.
An Aerodrome site in the Bow Valley, on the Indian Reserve at Morley was chosen as a base. A Bessoneau hangar was erected in August, and patrols were maintained throughout September and October with excellent results. DH 9A and Avro machines were used. The high speed and reserve power of the former are very valuable in that district, as strong winds are very prevalent and less powerful machines cannot make headway against them. With the co-operation of the Radiotelegraph Branch, Department of the Naval Service, a wireless service between machines on patrol and the base was established. Though the season of greatest fire hazard was over before flying commenced, many fires were reported,'and full information as to their exact location, extent and
 .	/
progress was supplied to the Forestry authorities.
The Superintendent of Dominion Parks and the Forestry Officers of the Commission of Conservation, as well as the Chief of the Forestry Branch, have expressed themselves fully satisfied with the results obtained by the introduction of the Air Patrol; they have ask that the services be extended, and that additional patrols be employed this year.
The base of this operation is being changed, this year, to High River, Alta.
Constructional cost to date	$ 1,000 00
Operational cost to date	 45,840 48
I have memoranda on all the stations, but I do not know whether they are of sufficient interest to hon. gentlemen for me to read them.
What does the minister mean by "control from the air?" Is there any application of fire extinguishing elements in connection with the air service?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No. I know of no control except to discover and locate fires and report them. I suppose the aeroplanes could land if suitable landing places were available, but that is not the object of the survey.

I understand that of the amount expended last year only $35,000 was for provincial purposes, and was divided on a fifty-fifty basis. I should like to know what posisible reason there is why the provinces should not pay in full the moneys -expended for their own particular puprposes. I can understand why there should be co-operation with the provinces so long as we have these aeroplanes, but I do not understand why when we do discharge certain duties for them we are not repaid the whole cost.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I suppose the matter was in an incipient stage when it was taken up last summer and the Air Board wanted to demonstrate what it could do, while the provincial authorities - may have been a little sceptical. At any rate we thought we had established a fair bargain as the work done was in the general interest of Canada.
I understand this is provincial property that we are guarding.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Only part of it-not in the West.

For instance, the province of Quebec has more money than the Federal Government has or will have for some considerable time to come, due I suppose to the fact that we have had twenty- * five years of good Liberal administration there. Why should we go to the assistance

of an authority highly solvent while we are on the brink of bankruptcy? It seems to me we are doing something which we have no right to do, and that we ought to protest vigorously against it. The province of Quebec needs assistance from no authority, and probably next year it will have a large surplus which it will be prepared to lend to the Federal Government at a fair rate of interest. I have not heard from the minister any valid reason why we should assist an authority which does not require our assistance. The property which is being preserved in this way belongs peculiarly to the province of Quebe. When the provincial authorities sell these timber limits they do not divide their profits with the Federal auhorities, and why in the name of everything that is sane and sensible we should be called upon to assist the province in any way is something that I cannot understand.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It may be that the matter should be reconsidered to see if we canont charge a higher proportion, if not the whole, of the cost to the provinces who request us to do the work. Quebec has gone into this work, I think, to a greater extent than any of the other provinces. It welcomed the idea, and we have gone ahead and demonstrated what civil aviation can do. As far as I know we have not done any fire ranging, only surveying and reporting on timber, water powers and the like, but the work has been pretty largely for provincial purposes-
Precisely.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: -and it might be well for us to reconsider whether we should continue the work unless the provinces pay the whole cost. However, last year we went into it on a fifty-fifty basis. We have not actually entered into any agreements this year, and that matter might be worth considering. There are provinces where all the natural resources belong to the Dominion; of course that would be a different matter.

Has the minister given any consideration at all to the question of cutting down this Estimate? It would seem that the heads of the branches in each department come to a decision as to how many men they can employ; they make recommendations accordingly to the minister, and the minister simply adopts them. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) could tell us how soon we shall be in a position to
employ everybody in Canada, taxing ourselves accordingly. It seems to be the object of the Government to get to that position as soon as possible. I am sure that we could save several hundred thousand dollars on this vote without doing any harm to the people; on the contrary, a substantial reduction would result in a great deal of benefit to the people.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think I can honestly say that I did use the pruning knife on this item.
Use it some more.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The expenditure under this head will have to progress with time; if we are to keep up with all the modern inventions that come out we must prepare for a considerable increase from year to year. We did not increase it this year; as a matter of fact, we cut down the personnel and stopped seventy-five per cent of the proposed operations. The figures ran to about four millions {before the pruning knife was applied. At the present figure I think we have cut down pretty nearly to the limit, if we are to go on at all. It may be the view in some quarters that we should not go on at all. I myself think that now that we have started it would be unwise to stop at this time. We can progress for a while, anyway, and see whether some real result is not accomplished. I believe that in civil aviation the results already obtained justify the expenditure. It has been intimated to me that last autumn fires which might have cost us several millions of dollars were located through these civil air operations and promptly extinguished.
Where?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In the West, at the mountains. It is possible that these fires might have been put out had we not had the civil aviation, but it is also possible that millions of dollars' worth of timber would have been destroyed. So that there is justification for at least part of the expenditure in actual saving to the country.
The minister intimates that the civil aviation is to be credited with certain valuable services. Now, what service does the Canadian Air Force render to the country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Just the same service as our militia render to the country. You cannot maintain an army or anything approaching it, you cannot maintain a military or naval system of any kind, if you

have not an air force in connection with it. The late war demonstrated, I think, to the satisfaction of everybody, even to the ordinary lay mind, that it was absolutely impossible to operate troops without an air service. All scouting is done by the air service now. All artillery work is directed by the air service, as well as all movements of troops. If you are going to maintain any form of militia at all, you must have some air service in connection with it; otherwise your army would be very little use in time of trouble.
Does the $800,000 for the Canadian Air Force bear the usual proportion to total military expenditure?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.
Is it greater or less?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Ours is much less.
Speaking from memory, I think the proportion of air expenditure in the United [DOT] States is 20 per cent of their total military expenditure, and in England I think the proportion is less than 20 per cent.

In this appropriation
there is an item of $825,000 for the Canadian Air Force and $700,000 for civil aviation. Is it not possible that either one of these branches might be dispensed with entirely and the training necessary in case of emergency made available through one of these two sources?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not think that
would work out satisfactorily. There is one matter I omitted to mention: the Civil Aviation Branch has, of course, charge of the training of all airmen, the granting of certificates, and the prescribing of all flying conditions. That branch is already kept busy with applications of various kinds. Regulations are passed prescribing the law under which all flying is done in Canada. Just at the moment there is an anomaly in the condition between Canada and the United States. Canada, having become a member of the League of Nations, is bound by .certain general regulations applicable to all nations which became parties to the covenant. In the meantime we are providing our own regulations' and have notified the United States authorities that their machines flying over Canada must comply with our requirements, notwithstanding the fact that the United States has not become a member of the League of Nations.
To what extent is Canada bound in this matter by her membership in the League, of Nations?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Canada has given her
assent as a signatory to the covenant of the League of Nations to certain general air rules applicable to all members of the league, and not applicable, of course, to the United States, which has not become a member.

The minister has told us
that he is maintaining an air station at or near the city of Halifax. So far as I can learn, that station is absolutely useless, either for commercial or for military purposes. There may be four or five aeroplanes or seaplanes situated there, but they are of no use to the people of Canada. I am sure that the people of Nova Scotia have no desire for an air force or for aero-pldnes either in Halifax or anywhere else on the coast of that province. I would like to ask the minister how many accidents occurred during the year 1920, fatal or otherwise.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I could not say with
any exactitude. I think there were about eight or nine accidents, three of them fatal, if I remember rightly. Later in the evening I can get the exact number for my hon. friend. The secretary of the Air Board is not in the city this afternoon, but he will be here to-night.

It seems to me that this is a pretty high price to pay for an air service in peace time. If we had war, of course it would be necessary to keep our air service and we would expect to have accidents. But it is a crime to render our very best young men, those from 21 to 25 years of age, liable to be killed or dangerously injured, just for the sake of having in Canada a service which is absolutely unnecessary. I protest against it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would direct the attention of the committee to the fact that there is an item in this appropriation for contingencies, $25,000. I would ask the minister what amounts are required for the purposes of contingencies that could not be taken out of the vote for Civil Aviation or for the Canadian Air Force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The appropriation last year for this was $50,000. The memorandum which I have is this. This larger amount was necessary on account of organization work which was then going on and which will be dispensed with this year. The expense incurred under this vote will not be so great this year as during the organization period, when no stock of

printed forms, etc., was available. Last year we had to do all that work. In addition we paid temporary employees, and for the present year it is not expected that there will be so many temporary employees as there were last year as the permanent staff has now been organized.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We have
voted for civil aviation $700,000 and for Canadian Air Force $825,000. We are not asking for any details. These amounts cover everything in connection with those forces. Why then should we vote $25,000 for contingencies? The items which my
5 p.m. hon. friend has mentioned in regard to last year could have been spent under the general appropriation; I do not think they should be under contingencies, and unless he can show good reasons why they cannot be spent under the general appropriation either for the Canadian Air Force, or for civil aviation, I think the item for contingencies should be struck out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I would have to consult with the officers of the board in regard to the matter. I presume this vote is to cover just such matters as I mentioned, printing and stationery, temporary employees, travelling, incidental expenses and the like. I cannot imagine what else the vote is for. If my hon. friend desires further information, I can get it for him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the
minister think any of the items which he has just mentioned could be met out of the vote for civil aviation or the vote for the Canadian Air Force? If he does, this vote for contingencies should be struck out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not believe they could, because these appropriations are pared down even to a dollar. These are the details of the $825,000 item:
28-day refresher course for 190 flying
officers	$380,000
28-day refresher course for 50 ground
officers	 22,000
Three months' course for 400 mechanics	 240,000
Spares	 100,000
Seaplane training	 60,000
Provincial executives, C.A.F. Associations	 23,000
Total	$825,000
Those are right to a dollar without any room for contingencies. I have not the items for civil aviation, but I know the basis on which the appropriations were made up, and I know there is not a dollar left over unless there was a special item
for contingencies, so closely was the expenditure pared down.
By whom are the items made up?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
By the vice-chairman
and the secretary.
Who are the members of the Air Board? What salaries are they paid? What are the expenses?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am the chairman of the board. Col. O. M. Biggar, K.C., is vice-chairman.
What is his salary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Col. Biggar gets no
salary. Sir Willoughby Gwatkin is inspector general of the force. Lt.-Col. Leckie is director of flying operations. Lt.-Col. Scott is controller of civil aviation, Captain Hose is director of the Naval Service. Dr. Deville is surveyor general. Captain Hose and Dr. Deville receive nothing for their services. I think the salaries are $5,000 each for the three other officers whom I named. It may be that General Gwatkin receives more than that. I can verify that in a minute or two.
How is the distinction made between those who receive a salary and those who receive nothing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The other members of the board like myself and Col. O. M. Biggar, Capt. Hose and Dr. Deville are in other offices of the Government and receive other compensation.
Are the members of the board all Canadians?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That depends upon
what you call a Canadian. General Gwatkin is an Englishman, long resident in Canada. Captain Hose is an Englishman, resident in Canada. The others are Canadians.
, Mr. COPP: My hon. friend said that there was an appropriation of some $23,000 for provincial organizations. How is that distributed? Are there boards in the different provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There are nine pro-i
vincial boards, one for each province, and there is a certain amount of expense in connection with each board. This appropriation of $23,000 covers the expense of the nine boards.
Are there any salaries in connection with these boards? .

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are no salaries paid for the boards. They hold periodical meetings, and they have examinations of their men and things of that kind. Our officers attend the meetings from time to time for the purpose of conference and discussion.
This would cover travelling expenses and things of that kind?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, this covers everything.
Is there any co-operation between the two branches of the service?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
They are kept separate, but one board presides over them both. Their duties are, of course, separate. One is purely military and naval.
Mr. EULER Is a man ever transferred from one branch to another?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A man may be transferred, but none of the officers.
What about equipment?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Certain equipment is suitable for military and naval purposes and certain is not suitable for that. In matters of repairs, civil aviation machines are repaired by the military repair shops.
Who comprise the Nova Scotia Aviation Board?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not believe I could give the names. The Lieutenant Governor is president of it.
He is a flier all right. .

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He is chairman of the board, reputable citizens named by the provinces themselves comprise the boards. We have nothing to do with the selection of them.

Are they gentlemen who have any knowledge of aviation, or are they appointed on account of some other qualifications? I am speaking only for my own province, because I have some knowledge of the work that has not been done in regard to aviation in my province. It is not necessary to have this aviation board or any aviation in Nova Scotia. I should like the minister to tell the committee what work was done in Halifax last year before we are asked to pass an appropriation, a portion of which is to be spent- in Nova Scotia. As far as my knowledge goes, not one dollar of benefit resulted in 1920 from either a war or a civil standpoint. I doubt if five people in Nova Scotia can say that they ever saw an aeroplane or a hydroplane during 1920,

and before we are called upon to vote a large amount of money to maintain a station in Nova Scotia, we should be satisfied that some beneficial result has been obtained. As far as my knowledge goes, it is an absolute waste of money to have this station in Halifax.	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The board is for the Maritime Provinces, not for Nova Scotia. These are the members of the board: His Honour the hon. Wm. Pugsley, Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick; His Honour McCallum Grant, Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia; His Honour M. McKinnon, Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island; J. O. Hyndman; W. H. Dennis; Pilot Officer A. E. Stephenson; Flight Lieutenant R. A. Logan, C.A.F.; Flight Lieutenant J. L. M. White, D.F.C.; Flying Officer A. McGregor, D.F.C., C.A.F.; Pilot Officer H. H. Whitlock, C.A.F.; Secretary, Flying Officer H. R. Stewart, 57 Grafton Street, Charlottetown, P.E.I.
The station in Now Scotia is considered as absolutely essential for the purpose of a seaplane service. The naval service nowadays must have as an adjunct a seaplane service, and the best base for that on the eastern coast was considered to be at Halifax in Nova Scotia, and on the west in British Columbia. These are our two seaplane stations. They are kept up very inexpensively at the present time, and our hope is that they will justify the money we are spending on them.

The minister has given us the names of the members of the Air Board for the Maritime Provinces, and I notice that some very estimable gentlemen are members of that board. The Lieutenant Governors of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are members of the board, and I think perhaps no gentlemen are held in higher esteem in the Maritime Provinces than the gentlemen who occupy these positions at the present time, but I think everybody will agree with me that these gentlemen know nothing about aviation. They are on the board, I presume, simply on account of their high official position. I presume that the other members of the board are members of the aviation corps. So far the minister has not given us any reason why this station should be continued. It no doubt is quite proper to have such a Ration in time of war, and, of course, if a station has to be established, Halifax is the logical place on the eastern seaboard, and the station in the West must be in British Columbia, but at the present time I think there is absolutely no neces-

sity to have any air board or any expenditure on either of these stations. I think that no benefit has been derived by the people of Nova Scotia from having this station at Halifax during the past year or since the war. It is quite true that during the war we had seaplanes in the province of Nova Scotia, but they were supplied to us by the American Government and were officered by American officers. They did good work. We had absolutely to depend on American officers to guard the coast of Nova Scotia during the war. I doubt whether you could find five men in Nova Scotia who knew that there was a seaplane in or near the city of Halifax in the last year or so, and I say there is absolutely no necessity for maintaining this station at the present time.

How
many men were trained at Halifax station last year, and to what use is the station being put? I can well understand that Halifax would be an excellent base for such a station, but we would like to know what this station is useful for. Is it training men, or doing something that contributes to the defence of the country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is not a training station at the present time. All the work that is done up as far as Lake St. John, and, in fact, further west than that, is done by seaplane. All these seaplanes are assembled at Halifax and distributed from there. For instance, the ones that went to lake ' St. John came up the St. Lawrence to that place opposite Riviere du Loup. They made a landing there, and from there went on up the river a considerable distance, and then northward They have to depend upon lake and river landings. You cannot make a landing in the rough forest country at all. It is therefore absolutely necessary to utilize seaplanes. They are assembled at Halifax, and go back to Halifax at the end of the year. We have a staff of repair men there, but no training takes place at the station. The training, which is largely military training, takes place at Borden in the province of Ontario.
How many bases are there throughout the country, and what is the equipment of each?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not think I can give the exact equipment. We have a seaplane station at Vancouver in British Columbia, one at Morley in Alberta, one at High River, in Alberta, and we are equipping one for both airships and seaplanes near Winnipeg, Lake Winnipeg being the landing stage for the seaplanes. Coming easterly, we have a military base at Camp Borden, and a small establishment in Ottawa at Rockcliffe. We have one in northern Quebec, but from there east we have none until we get to Nova Scotia, where we have a seaplane station.
I thought the municipalities had some.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Those are landing stations, not bases. Some municipalites provide landing stations entirely at their own expense.
Are any aircraft used in Eastern Canada in connection with forest fires?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They are used in British Columbia, but I do not know whether they are used for this purpose in Eastern Canada. Airships are used in the Rocky Mountain section and in Northern Alberta, but I do not know whether they are used to put out fires in Northern Quebec. If aircraft are used for this purpose they are seaplanes.
In what part of Northern Quebec has the air force operated?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: From Lake St. John 250 miles north. W'ork was done there last summer, and this year they propose to operate from another lake, the name of which I cannot remember at the moment. The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux), will remember it.

speechtext: Item agreed to.

I move that
the committee rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again this day.
Motion agreed to: progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. R. W. Wigmore (Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Steele in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to constitute the Department of Customs, and Excise, and to amend the Customs Act and Inland Revenue Act, and to provide,-
1.	That there shall be a Department of the Government of Canada which shall be called the Department of Customs and Excise, over which the Minister of Customs and Excise shall preside; and the Minister of Customs and Excise shall be substituted for the Minister of Customs and for the Minister of Inland

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Revenue and for the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue whenever they or any of them are or is mentioned or referred to in any statute or in any regulation or order made under or in pursuance of any statute; and such other provisions shall be made as are necessary to carry out the proposed change in the constitution of the said Department, and that the Customs and Inland Revenue Act he amended in these respects.
2.	That section thirty-one of the Customs Act be amended by adding the provision that an entry shall not be perfect unless in all cases of shipments from any country other than the United Kingdom, British Colonies and British Possessions, where the value for duty of the invoiced goods in terms of the standard dollar of Canada is one hundred dollars or over, such invoice bear thereon a certificate of a Canadian Trade Commissioner, British Consul or other duly accredited officer, in the form or to the effect prescribed ^in that behalf by the Governor in Council, who may also prescribe the fee to be charged therefor.
3.	That section forty of the said Act, relating to the valuation of goods at their fair market value in the principal markets of the country whence exported, be amended by providing that such value in no case is to be lower than the wholesale price thereof at such time and place, and by the added provision that the value for duty of new or unused goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada, plus a reasonable profit thereon, and the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue shall be the sole judge of what shall constitute a reasonable profit in the circumstances.
4.	That section fifty-nine of the said Act be amended toy adding thereto the provision that notwithstanding any of the provisions of the section, in computing the value for duty of the currency of an invoice, no reduction shall be allowed in excess of fifty per cent of the value of the standard or proclaimed currency of the country from whence the goods are invoiced to Canada, irrespective of the rate of exchange existi-ng between such country and Canada on date of the shipment of the goods; and in respect of goods shipped to Canada from a country where the rate of exchange is adverse to Canada^ the value for duty of the currency of the invoice sljall be computed at the rate of exchange existing between such country and Canada at the date of the shipment of the goods.
5.	That section one hundred and four of the said Act be amended to provide that entry of goods outwards by land conveyance shall be made at the Custom-house of the port of exit for Canada.
6.	That section one hundred and thirty-two of the Inland Revenue Act, relating to the recovery of penalties, be amended to provide that the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court be extended to enforce penalties up to two thousand dollars, and that every action, suit or prosecution taken under the provisions of the Act shall be inscribed on a privileged docket or roll, and heard by privilege and preference.
7.	That section one hundred and eighty of the said Act be amended to provide that the certificate^ of a provincial analyst shall be accepted as evidence of the alcoholic content of the beer or wash suitable for the manufacture of spirits.
8.	That section one hundred and eighty-one of the said Act be repealed and in lieu thereof it be enacted that every person who has been convicted of an offence against the provisions of section one hundred and eighty, relating to
[Sir George Foster.j
distilling without a license, or has been adjudged liable to the penalty therein provided for, shall in addition to any such penalty, ^ incur a penalty in double the amount of duties which should have been paid.
'i. That the said Act be amended by the insertion of the provision that on every cask or barrel used in a brewery or for keeping or delivering out any beer, there shall at all times be legibly cut, branded or painted in oil colours on one head, the name and address of the brewer; and on every bottle containing beer, there shall at all .times be securely fixed by the brewer or bottler of the said beer, a label showing in conspicuous type the name and address of the brewer or bottler of the said beer and showing also the percentage of proof spirits contained in the said beer.
10. That section three hundred and fifty-six of the said Act be amended by adding the provision that every person who sells or offers for sale any manufactured tobacco or cigars otherwise than in or from the original package bearing thereon the proper revenue stamps, whether or not the proper duty has been paid on such tobacco or cigars, shall be guilty of an offence and-be liable to a penalty of not less than ten dollars and not exceeding fifty dollars and for a second offence to a penalty of fifty dollars.- The Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue.

maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The Department of
Customs and Department of Inland Revenue were combined by Order in Council in 1918, under the name of the Department of Customs and Excise. The Customs Act and the Inland Revenue Act each contained sections constituting the two departments. Briefly, the proposed Act provides a uniform law constituting the combined departments and defining the minister's duties, and at the same time provides for some minor amendments to the Customs Act and the Inland Revenue Act. It is proposed to change the title from "Customs and Inland Revenue" to "Customs and Excise", and to make corresponding changes throughout the two Acts.
The proposed amendments to the Customs Act are: (a) To provide for certificates of Canadian Trade Commissioners or Consular Agents on invoices from foreign countries; (b) To provide for valuation for duty for customs purposes in certain cases; (c) To provide for valuation for customs purposes of foreign currencies in certain cases; (d), To provide for licensing of Customs house Brokers.
The proposed amendments to the Inland Revenue Act are: (a) To provide for increased jurisdiction in proceedings by summary conviction; (b) To facilitate prosecutions under section 180 respecting illicit stills; (c) To provide for marking containers of beer with name of brewer or bottler and description, of alcoholic strength of contents; (d) To

facilitate prosecutions, under section 356, relating to unlawful sale of tobacco and cigars.

maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would like to submit
a word or two with reference to subsection 7 of the resolution which reads as follows:
That section one hundred and eighty of the said Act be amended to provide that the certificate of a provincial analyst shall be accepted as evidence of the alcoholic contents of the beer or wash suitable for the manufacture of spirits.
Now in Western Ontario it is a very common practice amongst the farmers in various districts to use molasses diluted with water in the ordinary everyday feed of their hogs. The production of hogs in western Ontario is a very staple industry with the farmers, and a case that came to my attention last year was in substance as follows: An excise officer from Toronto went up into the county of Huron, the county adjoining that which I have the honour to represent, and in districts of that county it was a very common practice to prepare molasses with water and to sprinkle it upon the hog feed, at a certain time during the fattening period to the great benefit of the animals and the improvement of the quality of the pork. This officer went to a farmer of good reputation, who had nothing against him, and who was following the practice not only of his immediate neighbours but of the farmers generally throughout the county. The officer found ten gallons of molasses and water in the farmer's barn, ripening there for the purpose of being used to feed his hogs. Now, speaking from memory, section 180 of the Act provides that a man having in his possession beer or wash out of which spirits could be made, is, upon being brought before a magistrate, liable to be found guilty from the mere fact of having that liquid in his possession, and the minimum penalty is $200. In the case in question the magistrate intimated that he was convinced it was a hardship but he could not help himself-the Act was so drastic he had to impose a fine. Under a decision of the Supreme Court of Alberta it had been found that there was summary jurisdiction to try a case and impose a fine under section 180; but that court finally reversed its own judgment and said there was no summary jurisdiction vested in a magistrate, and that a farmer, or any one having the wash could be tried by preliminary investigation, followed by an indictment before the court. I believe that is the law.
Now, it seems to me that one of the things this country is suffering from, to a certain degree at least, is the drastic nature of legislation of this kind under which the most innocent man is at the mercy of a zealous Inland Revenue officer who

without any case other than the fact that the man has such things in his possession

will pay a visit and find the mixture of the alcoholic content. Then under this section that is now proposed, all he has to do is to get the certificate of the analyst and the man is fined, or he is indicted and prosecuted, and then subjected to both fine and imprisonment without the option of saying a word. There is no escape except by an appeal, after conviction, to the clemency of the powers that be-to bring forward the case, and probably present the evidence, and ask for a remission of the fine. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that such drastic legislation should not be acted upon without very great care, and there should be some provision in the law which would enable the man, upon trial, to show that the mixture was on his premises innocently. Furthermore, if the jurisdiction is going to be changed, the magistrate in the case should have summary jurisdiction so that he might hold that in such an instance as I have mentioned the liquid was being retained for a proper and useful purpose. Under the circumstances, and entertaining such an opinion, the magistrate would have power to say there is nothing culpable by reason of having the mixture there. This is a very serious matter and in the district in question it has put fear and trembling into the hearts of the men who have followed for a lifetime the practice I have described. The practice is so common that merchants publish advertisements in the papers declaring that the farmers may obtain molasses for the purpose mentioned. It is not a creation of modern conditions; it has been in vogue for many years. Moreover, the miller who sells chopped feeds also advertises where molasses can be found. It seems to me, therefore, that I am right in asking that before this section is passed the minister should take some steps to amend the Act so that in cases such as I have described a man will be enabled to show his innocence and to escape conviction when there is no guilty intent. I bring this matter forward in the hope that the minister will get his departmental officials to consider this suggestion in the interests of the public, who are entitled to be safeguarded against any unwarrantable prosecution.

Going back to subsection 2, I should like the minister to explain how he is going to have, we will say, a trade commissioner to attend to the business of shipments from the United States when there is no such official as a Canadian trade commissioner among those 110,000,000 people. It does say, of course, that the British consul may act. ^ Well he may; but he may be at Washington, and the man who wants to ship goods, say, at Seattle, San Francisco or some other distant port will be greatly inconvenienced. We ought to have trade agents in the United States for the purpose of facilitating trade with Canada; instead of that we have such agents in countries 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 miles away.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As far as that section is concerned, the objection the hon. member raised does not apply at all.

speechtext: Section 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Section 7 of the resolution. This is just for the purpose of defining what is meant by the term "departmental analysis." maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What
did the Government do-collect tKe fine? Mr. WIGMORE: Yes.

maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it or is it not legal for a person under the regu-ations in Ontario to brew beer of more than two and a half per cent strength for his own use?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is a clause in the minister's regulations covering that, and that is why I have brought it to his attention. The regulations of the department do permit it. But how far does that conflict with the local authorities, and who has the greater jurisdiction?

maintopic: CUSTOMS AND INLAND REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should like to get information on a point, although perhaps it has not a direct bearing on what is now before the committee. Referring to subsection (c) of 180 we find the following:
nveiy person who without having a license under this Act, then in force,-
