Then if it means that I want to protest against it most emphatically. That seems to me to be a monstrous attitude to take. In the case that I have referred to, the man who was fined was a tinsmith. He was not asked to make the whole apparatus; if he had been he certainly would have known what he was doing. The guilty party came to him and asked merely for a certain part, a bit of piping, and the tinsmith made it. In my opinion-and I feel certain I am right as to that-he did it innocently, and it is not right that under those circumstances a man should be liable to penalty. If this law has the effect of making such a man liable to penalty even if the magistrate believes he is innocent, then I say it is not right, and I do think the minister should consider the matter. I was just wondering whether the insertion of the word "knowingly"' would be dangerous. I quite appreciate the fact that it might open the door to abuses, but I am not so sure that justice could not be done if that word were used in connection with this provision. A man charged with the offence may deny it, but if the evidence is such as to convince the magistrate that he did it knowingly, he can be fined; if the evidence is not sufficient to show that, surely he should not he fined. I am a little surprised now to hear that the department takes the view that under the set of facts which I have outlined a perfectly innocent man is liable to a very serious penalty. I do not think a law like that should stand, and I hope the minister will change it.

I would like to protest, as I have protested time and again in this House, against this unnecessary restrictive legislation. I have been making this protest for years and I am going to continue to do it. I do not blame the minister; I blame the officials who bring this stuff into Parliament.
Blame the responsible minister.

I say it is time we cut out this kind of legislation which restricts the rights of the people. Speaking in the House a few days ago I pointed out that under these various laws as they now stand a man does not know whether he is a law-abiding citizen or a criminal. We are loading up the statutes with provisions of these kinds, making innocent men guilty and giving them no recourse. I do not really know whether we are losing our moorings, whether we are departing from a condition of sanity or not, or whether we still have any rights left us under the old Magna Charta, the Bill of Rights and other things that our forefathers fought for. Legislation of this kind ought to be removed from the statute book at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: This is not new legislation; it has been on the statute book for years. The only change which is being *made is that we are taking the analysis of the provincial men as well as of the federal departmental man. As to the case mentioned by the member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys), I should think that the magistrate would deal with the merits of the case. I am not a lawyer, but I should think that if it was proved that the tinsmith was, absolutely innocent, he would not have been penalized.

What the minister said in answer to my question does not bear out what he says now; if it did I would have no complaint to make. If the attitude of the department is that a man who proves that he did this thing innocently is entitled to acquittal, then I have no objection to offer. My objection was to the interpretation put upon this section by the officer of the department who was in charge of the case, and by a very capable counsel who came from Toronto. They argued that it made no difference how innocent a man was; the mere fact of his making a part of the apparatus was sufficient to warrant conviction. That was why I asked the minister if that was the interpretation of the department, and I understood him to say

that it was. If so, I want to protest. I do not know whether at this stage I can move an amendment; I presume I could not as this is a resolution, and I presume the only time when I could move an amendment would be when the Bill is introduced. Perhaps I had better say nothing more now until the Bill is before the House because, while the word "knowingly" would be appropriate to the point that I am making, the matter should be carefully looked into. There are so many other things in the resolution that possibly the word "knowingly" used in a wholesale way would not be proper drafting. In paragraph (f) of section 180, the word "conceal" is used, and if a man conceals a thing, the word "knowingly" would be superfluous. Therefore, I would not wish to move that the word "knowingly" be inserted to apply through all these clauses. Without saying anything further now, I should like to suggest to the minister to consider the point which I have raised, and I Kvill reserve to myself the opportunity of possibly moving an amendment along this line when the Bill itself is introduced.

Just a word as regards the minimum penalty. While I would not advocate that a man should be fined under any circumstances, when he is innocent of any wrongdoing, that has happened and it will happen while the law is at present framed. The former penalty of $100 has been changed by an amendment to the Act to $200. If the minimum were brought down to say $10, in order to give a magistrate a chance, where he is bound to impose a fine, to realize the difference between innocence and guilt, the penalty would not be so severe. It is a disgrace to a man to be fined for an innocent act, his punishment is greater than the fine; but to many men the loss of this money would be a great hardship. Therefore, I would suggest that the fine be brought down to a moderate one, regard being had to the fact that magistrates are not corrupt; that they are endeavouring to carry out the law. Let them have a little opportunity of exercising their judgment as to the extent of guilt, and let them modify their judgment to the extent of imposing a smaller fine than $200 when they think a man is really innocent. On the whole, I believe the law should be so framed that a man who is undoubtedly innocent should not be at the mercy of any magistrate or court.

I should like a little information on clause 2, which provides:
That section thirty-one of the Customs Act (be amended by adding' the provision that an entry _shall not be perfect unless in all cases of shipments from any country other than the United Kingdom, British Colonies and British possessions, where the value for duty of the invoiced goods in terms of the standard dollar of Canada is one hundred dollars or over, such invoice bear thereon a certificate of a Canadian Trade Commissioner, British Consul or other duly accredited officer,
I think that provision will work a hardship on both importers and exporters. I know some places where it is impossible to get a British consul or a Canadian trade commissioner to perform this service, and even where they are available, I do not see what good it is going to do, though perhaps the minister may have some explanation that will satisfy the committee. Vessels coming from the Mediterranean, for instance, with salt call at an island named Torrevieja and at another named Iviza, at neither of which is there a British consul or Canadian trade commissioner. If a vessel laden with salt goes to these islands and then comes to a Canadian port, I presume that the cargo would not be allowed to be landed here, or that the owner or importer would get into trouble. Even where there is a British consul, he would not know the value of the goods, and his certificate would not mean that the invoice was correct. I cannot see what good it is going to do, and I believe that it will work a hardship on both importers and exporters.

That is a
clause which will not be brought into effect except by proclamation, and the proclamation will not be issued until arrangements have been made to avoid any undue difficulties such as my hon. friend has suggested. I quite agree with the hon. member that if it were immediately brought into effect it would entail hardship, but we are going to avoid that in the way I have just said.
With reference to the person signing the certificate knowing or not knowing the value of the goods, there is no burden placed on the person who signs to find out what the prices of the goods are. All that the person who certifies has to do is to certify that the three copies are exact copies of the original, as to nrices, and the quantities and kinds of goods. That system

is in operation in the United States and applies to all exports from Canada, with the exception of goods less than $100 in value. The fee that the United States Government charges for this certification is a flat rate of $2.50 for the invoice certificated.
With reference to other countries, all of the South American countries, with the exception of perhaps two, have a system of certification of export invoices, on the same basis, but with varying charges. In some cases a flat charge is made, and in others a percentage charge of the value of the invoice, the minimum charges being in nearly all cases higher than those charged by the United States. Of course, when it is a percentage charge of the value of the invoice, it sometimes amounts to a pretty large figure. A large number of the European countries have a similar system, and they make it obligatory that these certificates shall accompany the invoice, and there is a charge therefor. This provision in our resolution is not to apply to any British country, either to the Old Country, or to any of the overseas dominions, colonies or dependencies. The ultimate object of it is to arrange for a system of trade representation as wide as we can possibly make it. It is not possible to put this into force with reference to the United States until we are in position to put it into force with all other foreign countries; otherwise, we would be discriminating against the United States, and we do not propose to do that. Consequently, at first we shall invoke the good services of the British consular and commercial intelligence officers in all these foreign countries for the purpose of certification, and gradually we shall work up, in the most important points, at least, to the establishment of a system of capable Canadian commissioners, who besides doing mere certification- that is only one part of it-will represent Canadian interests and try to expand Canadian trade. The matter has been engaging the attention of my department for a number of years, but was interrupted by the outbreak of the war, and has not been pursued since. The imposition of the small fee for certification of export invoices affords to the United States in so far as its whole consular service is concerned, an income under present rates which is quite sufficient to carry the whole expense of their consular service, and it is supposed, and I think rightly, that in the course of time it will be possible for Canada through the revenue that it thus obtains to put 
out well equipped and thoroughly efficient trade brigades, so to speak, in all the principal countries of the world, and to do that without the heavy outlay that we would have to meet ;f we did not charge a fee.
Some people may say that the fee itself acts as a tax on the consumer. It may be that sometimes it does, and it may be that sometimes it does not; that varies according to circumstances. It is, however, a very small fee, and where the invoices are for a. large amount the small sum of $2.50 for certification is a very, very trifling charge upon the value of the goods.
What immediate good does the minister hope to derive from the imposition of this fee? Is it with the object ultimately of extending Canadian trade, or what is the purpose of it?

I rather have missed what I started out to do, because I was flattering myself that I was explaining the purpose of it. The purpose of it, to take another tack and come up even with my hon. friend, is this: It is to enable Canada to extend into every quarter of the world where it is possible for her to do trade, the distribution of information, through trade agents, trade commissioners, and trade representatives, who will be appointed for the different places, and who will not only distribute information with reference to Canada but,-which is more important,-will gather information as to where, and of what kind, and to what extent there are trade possibilities and trade openings for Canadian products of all kinds, industrial and otherwise.

I suppose
my right hon. friend will say that it is for that purpose that the United States exacts a similar fee against Canadian exporters to that country. I do not think that is the purpose at all. I know that in my own province there are a great many American consular agents in different localities, and as a matter of fact, they are not Americans, but Canadian citizens.

They are all Canadian
citizens except one.

Yes, and they represent the United States, or the American consul at Ottawa or Halifax, or elsewhere, as the case may be, where there is a resident consul. These men represent the consul when any citizen of the United States requires the assistance or promotion of tko

United States Government. These officers are not appointed for the purpose of extending trade. The United States, of course, has a special line of officers known as trade commissioners, scattered throughout the world, hut I fail to see how we could hope to extend our trade by having someone whose duty it is to add a certificate to an invoice representing an export of goods. We can never hope, for centuries, to have consular representatives resident at all the ports in the countries to which we export. I do not think my hon. friend has the right idea in mind. The purpose he states is not the purpose of other countries in having a similar arrangement.

I grant that
the United States have consuls and consular trade representatives of different kinds. The two things are conjoined. I am quite certain-

think that after all these benefits are very much exaggerated?

Well, that is
the opinion of my hon. friend-
Mr.- MACLEAN:	I was merely asking
you.

- and if it pleases him it does not displease me. Now there is a very considerable burden in bearing the expenses of trade commissioners in every part of the world in which we consider it well to have our trade represented, and the small fee that will be charged makes it possible to gather a fund which will allow Canada to increase her trade representation very, very largely and without a burden upon the finances of the country. In these days, when representation abroad is growing all the time more expensive, to pay a trade commissioner, with his staff and his necessary help, in a city in a foreign country takes a very tidy sum of money. It is possible for Canada, by this arrangement, to obtain from the revenue from certifications a sufficient sum of money to enable her to go far beyond her present representation in trade in foreign countries, and to do that without burdening her own exchequer. That, therefore, is a point to be taken into consideration.

I will not provoke
further discussion from my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), because I am of the opinion that he will never put this clause into force for many years to come, and I am willing to let it go.
We will try it out. I am going to live long enough to put it into force, and I invite my hon. friend to live as long to see its operation.
Let us hope that it will be a long time before it goes into effect.
I hope my hon. friend will be here at the time.

I cannot see how the minister can expect, from the fees he may collect, through consular agents, from exporters of goods, to pay the cost of trade commissioners in different parts of the world. The United States has, in this country, and

elsewhere, what are known as consuls and consular agents. The member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), has pointed out that the consular agents are usually Canadian citizens, just as, abroad, they are citizens of the countries in which the United States is represented. For instance, while in Ontario the consul general is an American citizen, practically every consular agent in every town in Ontario or Nova Scotia, or in any other province, is a Canadian citizen. These men are paid half the fees they collect. The minister said that the fee was $2.50. He will not mind my correcting him. It used to be $2.50, but now, owing to the high cost of living, and the American exchange against Canada, it is $2.85. The charge for certification is $2.75, and there is 10 cents added for exchange. Of that $2.85 the local agent gets one-half, and the other half he remits to the agent in the centre of the province who, in turn, remits it to Ottawa. Now in my opinion it is impossible for Canada to appoint agents in all parts of the world. That will cost this country a great deal of money. I cannot see why it is necessary to enact this legislation at the present time unless it is going into force immediately. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just announced that he would not put it into force immediately; consequently, I cannot see the advisability of passing this clause in the resolution. As I said a few moments ago, there are certain places where there are no British consuls, or consular agents, or Canadian agents-in fact I am afraid that even the present trade commissioners which Canada maintains in certain parts of the world, or in certain foreign countries, are not doing very much good. Only a few days ago I was talking to the captain of one of the steamers in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and I asked him where he had made his last trip. He said he had been down to Buenos Aires and I then inquired if he had met the Canadian Trade Commissioner there. He replied that he had not, and that he did not know there was such a person.
I tried to find out from him if there was a Canadian agent at Buenos Aires, and he said he had been there three weeks and had never seen or heard of him. If that is the kind of trade agents the Government has appointed the quicker it recalls them the better. What I started out to say was that I do not think this is wise legislation to go into effect because it is going to be a great interference not noly with the businessmen of this country but with 
those in countries from which we import goods. At the present time, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows, the exporter from a foreign country sends to the importer three copies of an invoice which is certified to. Those three copies have to go to the customs officer as soon as the goods arrive at the seaport or the place at which the vessel or train arrives. That should be all the information which the customs authorities or the Government should require. It is quite true, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, that of the American consular invoices which the Canadian citizen has to get before he can export goods one copy goes to Washington, another to the person to whom the goods are sold, and the third copy remains in the hands of the American consul or consular agent. It seems to me that if three copies of the invoice come to Canada and are deposited with the customs officer in the port where the goods are entered, that information should be sufficient so far as the Canadian Government is concerned. I would strongly impress upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is no necessity for the clause in question at the present time, in view of the great inconvenience that is going to result from it to both exporters from foreign countries and to Canadian importers.

I want to impress upon my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that I do not think it is a wise thing for him to stand up in Parliament-I am not lecturing him at all, I am just stating how it strikes me-and throw cold1 water upon any trade commissioner, or the whole system of trade commissioners, because a friend of his tells him that he actually spent three weeks in Buenos Aires and never met a trade commissioner belonging to Canada. From that statement my hon. friend draws this conclusion: If that is the kind of trade commissioner you have abroad, you had better not send any abroad. That is not a fair position for my hon. friend to take. What was the matter with that man who spent three weeks in the little country of Buenos Aires?
It is a big country.

Where did he spend that time? One trade commissioner cannot go all over Buenos Aires in three weeks. My hon. friend states that his friend did not see a Canadian trade commissioner after being three weeks in the great country of the Argentina, but I am not going to take that as a condemnation

of my trade commissioner, particularly as we have in Buenos Aires as live a trade commissioner as we have in the whole outfit-a good man, an excellent man, one who understands the work and was there for a long while under Mr. Pousette years and years ago. AVe have kept that officer there, he is now our trade commissioner, and he is a good man. I am hound to stick up for my trade commissioners against such evidence as my hon. friend has given me. Then again my hon. friend says: "You are not going to put this system into force right away. What is the use of it unless you do put it in force right away?" Well, we have to provide for putting a thing into force before it becomes effective. My hon. friend, I believe, is somewhat of a fisherman. I imagine he does not wait until his vessel is ready to go out at the proper season before he gets his twine, and his lines, and his proper apparatus together. He makes his preparations, and we have to make our preparations. It is no slight thing to make proper preparation to put a system like this into force throughout the world. It is possible we will have it in operation inside of six months, and that is what I think I can say to this committee will be done. It takes a little time to do, but I am quite sure it will be done.
I have already communicated with the British authorities, and the Secretary of State for the Colonies has intimated his complete willingness to put me in touch with all the British consuls, consular officers, and intelligence officers throughout the world, and have them co-operate with me in this. That gives you an opportunity, without having to place Canadian commissioners in every part of the world before you can bring the system into operation; it gives you a modus operandi to facilitate your operations.
Now my hon. friend says we will not get much revenue from it. Suppose we test it by the facts? The United States last year got $496,184 in fees on the exports that were sent from Canada into the United States. Well, it is possible, I think, to make a rough calculation on that, and to come to the conclusion, without refining it very much, that we can get a good, tidy fee from this source. I am free to confess that when I first commenced looking into this question I was not very much in favour of the proposition. But the more I look into the matter, and the more the keenness of competition all over the world becomes apparent, the more I
feel that we must put forth more effort in order to help our Canadian producers, industrial and otherwise, to find markets outside for the surplus they produce. I have come to the conclusion that not only will it result in a great gain in commercial information, but it will also help us to represent Canada in a way we could not otherwise do, and to pay for it by this system of a small fee for the certification of invoices. My hon. friend took exception to the amount I stated as the fee in the United States. The fee is $2.50 in the United States. My hon. friend shakes his head and says "no," but that is exactly what it is-no more and no less. The man who pays that fee down there pays $2.50 in American money. If there is an exchange against Canada that exchange is applicable not merely to that fee but to all our trade.	.

I want to congratulate the minister upon what I conceive to be a forward step along the lines of increasing Canadian trade in foreign markets. It may be interesting to the House to know that while at present we have no trade agency in the United States, Great Britain maintains a complete corps there. At Washington there is the Commercial Counsellor to the Embassy. In addition there are consuls-general located at Boston, New York, Philadelphia. Chicago, New Orleans and San Francisco. There are also consuls and vice-consuls in those cities and at other points throughout the country. The total number of British representatives in the United States at present is 115-none from Canada. They are there largely to promote British trade. There are 49 foreign consuls in the city of New York alone, including representatives of the smaller South American republics. Argentina has a consul-general at New York and another at San Francisco; in addition she has a consul at New York and another at Norfolk, Virginia, and twenty vice-consuls at various points. Belgium has sixty consuls and commercial agents in the United States, Bolivia has thirteen, Brazil has forty, Chile has one consul-general in New York and fourteen consular officers; France with less trade than Canada, has consuls-general at San Francisco, New Orleans and New York, and also a full complement of consular officers; Norway has an excellent consular organization in the United States with a personnel of over fifty, including one consul-general at New York. Practically all these trade

representatives collect fees in the United States for viseing invoices or export manifests to their respective countries. The fees vary: Mexico and Ecuador charge 3 per cent on the invoice value; Peru, Bolivia and Guatemala, 2 per cent; France, $2.40; Japan, $4.00; Italy, $3.89; Spain, $12; Norway, $2.70.
The United States has a consular service throughout the world, including Canada, and all her consuls-general and consuls are paid by salary and are divided into classes. The only class referred to hy hon. gentlemen opposite who get their remuneration from fees, to the extent of one-half the fees they collect, are those of the minor branch of the service in Canada. Those of the major branch get salaries ranging from $12,000 a year down to $5,500-not very large salaries for the class of work they do. Their vice-consuls are divided into three classes, with remuneration ranging from $3,000 to $2,500. None of these officers are entitled to retain the fees which they collect; they are paid a straight salary. The total number of United States consular agents in Canada is 92. They are not here for nothing; they are here for the benefit of the United States upon a trade basis, and that fact alone ought to be illuminating to us in Canada, when we consider that with a population of eight or nine million here the United States thinks enough of this small market-small to-day, but which will ultimately be great-to keep here 92 consuls, vice-consuls and trade agents. It does seem very difficult to explain to the business man that that being so, we have not one agent to look after our export trade in that market of 110,000,000 people.

Are those 92 American
citizens, or are they partly Canadian?

The majority are
American.

How many are American
and how many are Canadian?

All I can say in answer to the hon. gentleman, because the nationality is not given in the repository where I got my information, is that I was told by the American consul-general here that they sometimes appointed Canadian citizens in small places aside from the larger avenues of trade.

Is it not a fact that in most of the outports the United States representatives are all Canadian citizens, those 
of American nationality being confined to the capitals of our provinces and other large centres?

I put on record in this
regard recently a statement that the full list of American consuls and agents in Canada can be found in the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs for 1920 in appendices A and B. It will be found that the United States has trade representatives from Halifax to Vancouver, mainly, of course, at points of importance. For instance, they have three or four in Montreal, in Toronto, and in Vancouver, and two or three in Halifax. What are they there for, is the point. Are they there to benefit Canada or to benefit the United States? Why, absolutely for the purpose of stimulating United States trade in Canada, to advise their home government regarding trade opportunities here, and through them their home industries.
And we are paying.

Exactly, we are paying for that service here to the extent of our manufacturers and producers paying the fees on all the invoices coming before the American consuls to be vised. It seems to me that if they can make a profit in eight years of more than $869,000 over and above all their overhead expenses in a market of eight or nine million people, surely Canadian agents over there with the larger market of over 100,000,000 people would correspondingly make their offices pay, in fact make them self-supporting out of the fees paid by the American importers, to say nothing of the advantage accruing from the information they would send our manufacturers and producers of American needs for gooffs made in Canadian factories by Canadian workmen. Surely that would be a step in the right direction, and the minister ds to be congratulated on what he has done. At a time when it is going to be harder to sell goods, the more information we can get of what the American people require the more will Canadian trade expand, and I am surprised at ihon. gentlemen opposite questioning for a moment the advisibility of such a pregressive step.
I appreciate that at the inception it might not be wise, as the minister has said, to put the service upon a complete basis, but it could be tried out. Points could be selected, having regard to the productions of Canada and the requirements for those productions in the markets of the United States, at which trade agentv could be ap-

pointed. Starting first with some bright up-to-date commercial travellers, young vigorous men understanding trade conditions, a limited service of these live wires might be tried out in the United States to give us the 'best information available as to the requirements of that market of 110,000,000 people. The tariff is going up, and, as the minister has said, we have got to be more active if we are to secure our share of the American trade; and undoubtedly we have great industrial establishments that need such export trade. To my mind this is one of the brightest features we have had for a long time, and I commend the minister very strongly for the progressive step he has taken, indicating as it dees, the intention of the Government to do everything possible to stimulate and develop the sale abroad of our surplus products. Already we sell to the United States $522,000,000 worth of goods, some wholly manufactured, some partly manufactured and the balance raw material, and they send us over a billion dollars worth of goods in return. Surely with the extent of the market over there in our favour, we can greatly extend our trade if this policy is carried out when we are already doing such a considerable volume of business without having any trade representatives in the United States.

I am sure we are all of one mind in regard to the expansion of Canadian trade, but when the hon. member for North Perth tries to argue that the fact of there being a number of American consular agents dn 'Canada, most of whom are Canadians, has any effect on Canadian trade, I 'am afraid I cannot agree with him. I venture to say that the American consular agents in this country do not increase trade from Canada to the United States $50,000 in one year. That is not there purpose at all-to try to sell Canadian goods to American customers.
It is not their purpose, but the information goes there and it is taken advantage of.

The whole argument of the hon. member for North Perth was that we should agree to this particular clause in the resolution in order that we might encourage Canadian trade. Now, I say that having these agents in the United States just as the Americans have them in Canada does not in any way encourage the sale of goods by Canada to the United States. I am heartily in accord with the idea of having Canadian trade commissioners in every foreign country, but the matter of having trade commissioners to facilitate the selling of goods is quite different from that of having agents to affix their certificate to goods coming from a foreign country. This resolution has nothing to do with the appointment of trade commissioners for the purpose of increasing trade. To my mind, its specific purpose is to inflict on exporters in foreign countries and importers in Canada something which is not at all in the interest of trade-in fact, entirely in restraint of trade. I know enough about the exporting of goods to the United States to enable me to say that the only purpose it will serve will be, as the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce says, to keep Washington in touch with the goods which are exported from the United States to Canada. I repeat that if this provision involved the appointment of trade commissioners I would be willing to argue strongly in its favour, because if this country is to go ahead and if we are to pay off our war debt we must have live representatives in foreign countries. But I am sorry to say that at present we have not got them, and while the gentleman who is in Buenos Aires may in the minister's opinion be-

My hon. friend is now making another statement; he is expressing his sorrow-deep sorrow, I am sure-that we have not live trade commissioners outside Canada. Now, will my hon. friend prove the things that he states and give the instances where we have inefficient trade commissioners? I am ready ta give the evidence of ten or twelve years' experience with the actual work of these commissioners, while my hon. friend has scarcely spoken, I suppose, to a dozen of them and understands nothing at all of what they are doing every day of the year. Do not let us have these general assertions. I do not say that a statement of that kind on the part of my hon. friend is going to knock the trade of commissioner-ship system into a cocked hat, but it is not right for a member of Parliament to make that statement-because we are all equally interested in having trade representation at its best-unless he puts up the proof.
There is no necessity for the minister to get so worked up oyer this matter. I am just as much interested as he is in the foreign trade of this country; perhaps I am more interested in it than he is.
Then you must not be so thoughtless.
It is not a matter of being thoughtless; it is a matter of knowing what I am talking about, and I am afraid the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not know what he is talking about.
Give us what you know-come along.

My experience and the
experience of business men in Nova Scotia is that there are trade commissioners in foreign countries who do not do any thing to improve trade between Canada and foreign countries, and when the minister says they do he does not know what he is talking about. If these men in South America and the West Indies were competent they would keep in close touch with the business men of this country. We had a member of Parliament get up in this House a fortnight ago and tell us of a business man, representing the Ford Motor Company of Windsor, who had travelled all over Europe for sixteen months, and who in all that time did not come in touch with one commercial traveller or one trade commissioner representing Canada.
What does that prove?

If the minister's trade commissioners are such good men, certainly this man, who represents a very large firm doing a large business, would have come across some of them in France or in other European countries. Now, the minister twitted me a few moments ago with the remark that one of my friends had referred slightingly to his agent at Buenos Aires. The minister did not even know that Buenos Aires was not a country. Buenos Aires is not a country, I want to tell the minister; it is a city, and the largest in South America. And I want to tell the minister that it was not a friend of mine who told me this, it was one of the minister's own friends, the captain of one of the minister's own steamers, part of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for which the minister and his friends voted $70,000,000, and in connection with the operation of which a false statement was given us either by the company at Toronto or somebody else. The man who gave me this information said that he was in Buenos Aires for three weeks and that he did not see the Canadian trade commissioner and never heard tell of him. So that the minister need not try to put off on me any of the sins of his own officials, or his own captains.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said just now that the provisions embodied in this resolution would come into force only by proclamation. There is nothing in the resolution providing for that
The Bill will provide for that.

I imagine that some of us will not be here at the time when all these agents will have been appointed in all countries of the world to furnish these certificates for the purpose of expanding the trade of Canada. My hon. friend argues that the object of having a trade commissioner affix his signature to a certificate on every invoice is to furnish information. Well, the invoice has to go through the customs in any case and that information could be obtained through the Customs Department. I do not see, therefore, the need for this provision. But the point I want to make is this: ever since this Government has been in power I have protested against the vesting of all kinds of power in the Governor in Council. This resolution provides that an entry shall not be perfect until the invoice bears a certificate "in the form or to the effect prescribed in that behalf by the Governor in Council." Well, we know what the "Governpr in Council" means; it means the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue. As to the Governor in Council prescribing the form, I have no objection. I want the minister to give me a detailed explanation as to what he is going to determine shall be the effect of this signature on the invoice by the representative of Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the fee charged in the United States for this service was $2.50. Well, we do not know what the Order in Council will provide as to the fee we will pay. The Minister of Customs says that in the United States last year a revenue of half a million was derived from this source. I say that half a million is paid by the consumer. If this certificate would add1 anything to the validity or the genuineness of the invoice, well and good, but, as has been pointed out by the member for Lunenburg, how is the representative of Canada to know that the prices on the invoices are true and correct? He does not know; he simply puts down his signature and gets a fee of $2.50 to $3, which the consumer has to pay. On a large number of invoices in respect of goods of which the value for duty is over $100, that will amount to something. I

do not see the usefulness of a provision of this kind-unless it be that it will give the Minister of Customs or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whoever will have charge of the matter, the appointing of some men as commercial representatives to sign these invoices. As the member for Lunenburg has said, the member for Perth has shifted his ground. We are not criticising the advisability of having commercial representatives in various countries to show the advantages that may be had in trading with Canada, or the superiority of Canadian products, or what Canada can produce and supply to those countries. But from that to the point of having a man in a foreign country to affix a signature to an invoice which is sent by the man from whom the Canadian importer purchases, there is a long way to travel, and I do not see any necessity for this except, as I have said, to give the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, through the Governor in Council, an opportunity to prescribe or determine what the effect of the signature will be. I would ask the minister to explain why the words "or to the effect prescribed" are inserted in clause 2 of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The form of certificate to be determined by the Governor in Council is the same form exactly as is called for to-day under section 32:
With the bill of entry of any goods, there shall be produced and delivered to and left with the collector an invoice of the goods, as provided in the last preceding section, attested by the oath of the owner, and if the owner is not the person entering such goods, then verified by the oath of the importer or consignee, or, subject to the provision hereinafter made, some other person who may lawfully make such entry and verify such invoice, in the form or to the effect of the oath or oaths prescribed by the Gorvernor in Council in that behalf.
Why is that not sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Because it is deemed
necessary and advisable to carry out the regulations as laid down by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is the form that is being carried out by every other country in the world to-day; it is a check on invoices and also a means whereby we can get information as regards imports into or exports from Canada.
In what respect is this a better check or a greater safeguard than the system which prevails at present?

The reading of that section does not answer my question. I want to know the form. The minister may provide any form he desires so long as the language is not extravagant, and I suppose it would be criticised if it were. What do the words "or to the effect prescribed" mean?

Does my hon. friend understand exactly what is meant to he done? The form of the invoice which is to be certificated is an exact replica of the invoice such as is rendered now and has been rendered for all these years. It is not another paper that is made up and signed by the person who certifies it. It is a copy or three copies of the invoice itself. It is not a new creation; it bears simply the sign manual of the officer that this is an exact duplicate of the commercial invoice which is sent with the goods, just as is done now and has been done for all these years past. It does not add any force to the invoice at all because it does not change it in any way. But there is this in connection with it, that you get three copies of those forms sent in the different ways that they are sent to the different destinations, and you collect the fee for the work. That gives you the revenue necessary for extending our trade commissioners.
Would the Canadian importer not pay that fee?

The United
States at the present time have that system at work in Canada, and the argument is made that if the United States charge a fee of $2.50 in Canada on each export invoice, the Canadian pays the fee. Now the argument is taken that if you reverse that and we put into operation on that side the same system as the United States carry out in Canada, it is still the Canadian consumer who pays the fee. There must be something wrong in that kind of reasoning.
I would say that the cosumer pays in all cases.

The minister has not
answered my question, I never doubted that there were to be triplicate invoices or said that the signature would add to or take away anything. My objection is to the words "or to the effect prescribed" in clause 2, which reads:
A certificate of a Canadian trade commissioner, British Consul or other duly accredited officer, in the form or to the effect prescribed.

That means
simply this, that the accredited officer, whoever he may be, certificates the invoice in the form or to the effect prescribed by the Governor-in-Council.
If the effect is prescribed by law, that makes it perfect.
The officer cannot go beyond the original invoice. He certificates that that is a true copy of the invoice. That is all that the wording means.

Why should the Governor-in-Council reserve to himself the right to determine or prescribe what effect this shall have? Let the law say what the certificate is to be. Drop the words "or to the effect prescribed."

You must use such a form as will certify to you that this certificate is an affirmation of the original invoice. The wording may be redundant. That is the way in which it is drawn up by the law officer.
I want to know why it is drawn up in that way.

I had the misfortune not to hear the first portion of the discussion, and it is quite possible that the point to which I am about to draw attention has already been covered; if so, my hon. friend will have to bear with me.
When I heard the speech of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy)
I was under the impression that we were dealing with a resolution to provide for trade commissioners all over America, but I find that there is nothing of that sort in the resolution. The resolution does seem to imply that there are to be additional trade commissioners, because iti refers to the necessity of having these certificates given by the trade commissioner or the British consul. Has the point been considered how many of these new trade commissioners will be appointed for this purpose? Has my hon. friend come to any conclusion on that point?

What I face is a condition of things which opens up for the future through gradual expansion, an opportunity for a very wide extension of our Irade commissionerships. /No"' the

United States has in this country some 75 or 80 of these different agents, consuls, consuls-general, and otherwise, who cover the whole of Canada, the area of which is equal to that of the United States. Going on the assumption that for us to carry out this scheme thoroughly in the United States would require about an equal number, that would mean that Canada must have in the United States, sooner or later, 60 or 70 or 80 full trade commissioners, or agents who do part of the work of the trade commissioner, but not the whole work, and who receive a part of the fees, as my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has stated. It is impossible for us to engage such a large force at once, so we propose to utilize in the United States, taking that country, for example, the British consular service and the commercial intelligence service, and probably some agents as well, for the purpose of certification mainly, and not only as gatherers or distributors of Canadian trade information. In the gradual working out of the scheme we will come to the point ultimately where we will have Canadian trade commissioners, pure and simple, in the most important points in the United States, and we will work out with lesser officials, at less expense, the machinery necessary for this certification, which is to be general. So I cannot say how many we will have at first. It will require a good deal of care in selecting those who are to go, and it will take time to get properly qualified persons.

My hon. friend knows
that once it is well understood that he is going to appoint a lot of trade commissioners in the United States, he will have no lack of applications.
The applications are easy.

He will in all probability find that it is not so easy to resist the pressure as he imagines to-day. There is one important point in this matter which my hon. friend has not stated squarely and emphatically. This is a proposal to impose an additional duty on goods coming into this country from the United States; that is what it is. It proposes that a parcel of goods to the amount of $100 shall be taxed for a certificate. The amount of the tax is not stated; it is to be fixed by the Governor in Council; but my hon. friend, by way of illustration, has stated that in the United States the tax is $2.50 for the certificate. Assuming that he follows the practice there-and how many times these hon. gentlemen are pleading the example of the United States; it is amazing how much they are learning from the United States now, and how little they were prepared to learn a while ago-he will add $2.50 to a bill of $100. There is no question who pays all these taxes. Two-and-a-half per cent may not amount to anything, I may be told. Why, Sir, in the memory of my hon. friend, and some of those who are even'younger, a great change in the politics of this country took place on a question of two-and-a-half per cent. In 1878 the Mackenzie Government were asked to add two and a half per cent to the duties, and they refused to do it, and went out of office on a question of two-and-a-half per cent. My hon. friend without the slightest hesitation is going to add $2.50 to the duty on every $100 worth of goods comling in here from the United States. That is a direct tax on the importer.

I do not think my hon. friend would make a statement that does not square with the facts. The way he stated it would give a wrong impression to the country. He says that this charge will amount to two-and-a-half- per cent upon every $100 worth of goods.

Upon one hundred
dollars worth of goods.

That is correct. Let me say this:	If a person sends in a
present of jewellery, that is not a commercial transaction. But some of these invoices will amount to $20,000, $50,000, and $100,000. Now $2.50 on an invoice of $20,000 is only one-eightieth of 1 per cent.

The amount would be small on a large invoice, I admit. If anything I said conveyed the impression that this was a tax of 2i per cent on every $100 worth of goods, that was not my intention, and it is not in accordance with the facts, but be the amount large or small, this is an additional tax on goods coming in from the United States. Can it be that there is some concealed desire to add a little more protection to the manufacturer in this way? It is quite possible, it seems to me. That is the effect of it,	at	all
events.	What is the cause of it?
We have been doing without this thing for ages, and how have the public been affected? Has the business of the country suffered? Has the revenue been defrauded? I cannot see what need there is for this. My hon. friend has given no reason but the one, that they have it in the United States. Once

more the plea is that we must follow the American example. That is not an argument. There may be reasons which might make it defensible from the American standpoint, but that is by no means a sufficient argument as to why we should have it here. I have not heard any other argument put forward than that this arrangement exists in the United States; therefore, it should exist in Canada. If we have been getting along without this tax for all this time without any evil having been created, and if the revenue has not been defrauded in any way, and no public interests have suffered, why on earth do you put on this tax? It is for one of two things: either it is intended as additional protection to the home manufacturer, or it is designed to create a large army of officials. Whether or not my hon. friend starts out with that intention, he will find ultimately that he will be under pressure to appoint a large army of officials in the United States to carry on this work. No man in this House is more anxious than I am to cultivate trade with the United States wherever it can be shown that benefit is derivable, and whenever my hon. friend can submit any scheme whereby we may develop business with our neighbours to the south of us, I will commend him for sending agents there, although, as I stated on a former occasion, when my hon. friend agreed with me, the proximity of Canada to the United States is a reason why we should not have any considerable number of agents across the line. My hon. friend agreed with that view, as I expressed it only a couple of weeks ago, but once he opens the door to the employment of agents he will find that pressure will be brought to bear upon him to send over a large army of such officials. I have seen no evidence to convince me that this is needed for the trade of the country, and I do not think that we should enter upon a policy which will have for its object the providing of places for a large number of officials in the United States.

When a man ships
goods to the United States, he takes into account, in fixing the price, all the elements that go to make up the cost to him. When making up the bill of costs, he knows that he has to pay this $2.50, and he therefore charges it. Whether he puts it in one form or another, is immaterial. My hon. friend must not deceive himself; these things are paid by the consumer in the end. If anyone goes to New York and buys goods, the bill is made up with full regard to all the expenses which the merchant or manufacturer has to incur in any shape of form. He makes up his bill and includes the $2.50, and the consumer will have to foot that $2.50 in addition to the first cost of the goods. My hon. friend has given no reason for this proposal. What harm has come of the present arrangement? Has the revenue been defrauded? I have asked that question before, but my hon. friend does not answer it. I repeat:	what is the need?
My hon. friend says that the charge will not be heavy, and that the exporter will pay. Well, that is a disputable point, and I have shown that it is the consumer who pays. But waiving that for the moment, I submit that that is not sufficient reason. How is the trade going to be benefited? My hon. friend admits that no new invoice will be taken to the agent to be certificated. He will get the same invoice as the original, and he will simply put a stamp on it and charge $2.50. Well, what additional information will you get from that that will be of benefit to trade? There will be absolutely no additional information from that process, and I do not see any earthly reason for this proposal except that you will make jobs for chaps in the United States. I say once more that I do not object to sending men there when there is business to be done, but I do submit that no case has been made out in the present instance.

My hon. friend, I
am sure, does not wish to mislead anyone, but I certainly think that his remarks will have that effect. If his contention is correct, that the consumer in Canada will pay this particular duty, does not the consumer in the United States also pay the duty- my hon. friend calls it a duty or a tax- which is charged on invoices of goods shipped from Canada to the United States? Surely my hon. friend will not argue that, if the consumer in the United States does not pay the tax that is charged on invoices of goods shipped from Canada across the
line, the consumer in Canada will pay the $2.50 levied from the American exporter before he sends his goods over here.

I have no hesitation in saying that the American consumer in the one case, and the Canadian consumer in the other, pay the duty, as they always will have to do. You may put it on one side of the account or the other, but in matters of this kind the consumer will ultimately pay charges of this kind. In this case, I have no doubt whatever that the charge will ultimately come home to the consumer.
Will it be the American or the Canadian consumer?
The consumer will pay in either case.

About an hour ago, I ventured to break into the discussion to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question. I want to know in what respect the present system has failed to satisfy the requirements of the Customs Department, and in what regard the proposition put forward in this resolution will be an improvement on the system now in operation.

This is not designed at all in the interests of the Customs Department. The Customs Department has had for years its system of invoicing, of inspection, and of examination, and it remains exactly the same. It is not aided in that respect by this system when it goes into effect. This method simply says to the agent on the other side, whoever he may be, that he has to certify that the invoice presented to him is such and such, and then he has to dispose of the three copies of the invoice that he certificates in the way which is stated by the law. The purpose of this is simply to have a convenient arrangement so that you can have agencies fairly reasonably well distributed, without being a burden upon the treasury of the country, where the certificates can be got and attached to the invoices and sent on to their destination. The purpose in all this is to extend the trade commissionership work in outside countries and to raise, by the simple method of the fee per invoice, the necessary funds to do it. That is what this is for and nothing else. There are incidental advantages that will ensue. In the first place, there will come with each of these certificated invoices its duplicate and it will be in the hands of the Trade

and Commerce Department here showing the origin of the goods and the peculiar train, trend and current of these different transactions. In that way valuable information will be available to the department which it may use; but the main thing is to build upon this a body of trade commissioners in these foreign countries who will do the work that trade commissioners are doing now, only do it in a much more extended and in a much more widely distributed way.
Now, as to the tax that is proposed. You have, for instance, different kinds of transactions. Here is somebody in the United States who wants to send a present up to some friend in Canada. If the value does not go beyond $100 then there is no payment at all. If it goes beyond $100, payment has to be made for the certification of the invoice. That is not a tax on trade- that is simply what a man pays for sending something that he wants to be sent to a friend. That is one form of transaction. I think we can put that to one side. The number of transactions which are in the neighbourhood of $100, or such small amounts for which invoices are to be made out and sent into Canada, is comparatively small. The invoices are for larger amounts, sometimes very large amounts. On a $20,000 invoice the fee is only one-eightieth of one per cent, and I can hardly look upon that as a tax which is burdensome upon either consumer or shipper, whoever may have to pay it, and it is so small that it certainly could not make an item in the value of the goods which are sent. So that for a trifling burden, if it be a burden at all, we get the funds necessary for widely extending our Canadian trade commission-ership system which is asked for on both sides of the House, which is asked for by the business community as well, and which, from every side within the last four or five years, I have been persuaded and counselled to put into operation. We are asked for more men to distribute information with reference to Canada, and for more men outside who will gather information with reference to trade possibilities.
Now, my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) says that only two reasons have been given for adopting this policy, and one is that the United States does it. I have not in any degree based my argument upon that. I am not doing this simply because the United States does it. I have cited the fact that most of the countries in the world do it, that it is a

system that is generally in vogue, and , therefore we are not inaugurating a system that is not already in existence. Nor have I had the least idea of inaugurating a system of this kind, in order to make offices and places. You cannot have trade commissioners outside of Canada unless you appoint them, whether it is by this system or any other system. If you want more trade commissioners you have to appoint them, and the law as it exists to-day is that they are appointed through the Civil Service Commission. They will be appointed in just the same way as they have been

as prescribed by the laws which are in force for the time being.
Would they be technical officers under the new Bill?

We have not
received the new Bill yet.

I have listened with
very great interest to the lengthy explanation given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in answer to my inquiry, but I still fail to see the special reasons for the enactment of this new provision. If it is the intention of the Department of Trade and Commerce to extend this service, why not extend it along the lines that have already been inaugurated-that is appointing agents here and there throughout the world and paying them salaries from the public revenue? I quite agree with the claim made by the member for Shelburne and Queen's that in the last analysis the consumer will pay this charge, the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) to the contrary notwithstanding. In the case of goods purchased in Canada, exported to the United States, the commission or fee charged is paid by the purchaser on the other side. On the other hand in the case of purchases of merchandise in the United States made by a Canadian importer he would be compelled under this resolution to pay a fee of $2.50 for a certified invoice. Undoubtedly that charge will be included by the manufacturer in the cost of manufacturing his goods. Therefore the consumer in either case will have to pay that additional charge, the exchange upon it, and the duty as well. On Saturday afternoon we were discussing another item where an additional charge was 'made. This only goes to show that Government is continually adding to the cost of commodities. On Saturday the Minister of Finance caused a resolution to be passed under which each item of merchandise coming into this country will have to be

branded. Now that is going to be an expensive operation, and I repeat that in the last analysis the consumer will have to pay the cost. I defy successful contradiction of that statement. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt), challenged a statement made by the member for Shelburne and Queen's as to the added cost on $100 worth of merchandise. I think the position taken by them was correct to a certain extent; but the minister has claimed that by the operation of this resolution he will realize a revenue of at least $500,000. If that statement is correct there is no question in my mind but that the consumers in Canada will have to provide that money. Not only that, but in addition they will have to pay the customs duty on that $500,000 and the profits two or three times over on this amount. I claim that the system already in force whereby an importer of over a certain amount of goods must produce an invoice certified by the exporter, or by some one acting under power of attorney from him, gives to the Government of this country all the protection they require; in fact, it gives them all the protection they will have under this system, because there is no question in my mind that the trade agent it is contemplated to appoint will be nothing more or less than a rubber stamp. The exporter will pay him $2.50, and the trade agent will stamp the invoice-which is merely the excuse for collecting the fee. If the Government continues from day to day as they are doing now, the consumer will certainly realize before long why commodities are costing so much more in Canada than in other countries. If this policy proceeds very much longer, I would not be at all surprised if the people began to clamour for another committee to investigate the high cost of living, and after the responsibility is saddled unfairly on the retailers- as was done two years ago-we will no doubt have another Board of Commerce, and on its dying by the process of elimination and otherwise we will have perhaps some other combination to regulate trade. But more effective than any of these committees or boards would be some scheme whereby this Government could be induced to go to the country for a new mandate, for I am confident that the people would then put an end to all this nonsense.

Mr. Chairman,

I must say that I have failed to notice that my right hon. friend the minister has met the arguments of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. I would be very willing indeed to support my right hon. friend if I were sure that his proposal made for promotion of trade. My right hon. friend will readily believe that about me. For a number of years in this House I have not been troubling governments so much to promote trade as to persuade them not to prevent trade. That is my trouble with the governments of this country. Though my right hon. friend has persuaded himself that what he is doing is in favour of the promotion of trade, I am not at all sure but that his action will have a diametrically opposite effect. The Government does not need to promote trade. If governments would let peoples alone they would do all the trading that is necessary. It is as natural to a man to trade in a civilized country as it is for him to breathe; and we never think of helping him to breathe by putting him in tight corsets; but we do think of helping him to trade by putting obstacles in the way.
Here we have two countries with 3,000 miles of border line of an imaginary nature, and the peoples on the two sides of that line would trade freely with one another if they were left alone. They cannot be kept from doing it, because we all know, whether in the States or in Canada, people who live near the border line are all free traders by night when they can evade the tariff. We have this border line with the two peoples wishful to trade without any promotion from the Government. But the Government on one side of the line, misunderstanding the true nature of trade, said, "Now, this is an unnatural desire if it goes too far, so we will put up a barrier against those other fellows and prevent them sending stuff into our country." And the Government on the other side of the line says, "Well, we will put up a barrier on our side." So here we have the living waters of human production, which would supply the elements of trade in rich abundance on both sides of the line just as it suited the private requirements of the two peoples, and those waters ready to flow, but we have a double barrier by the efforts of the two Governments. Although each Government has a department of Trade and Commerce, presumably for the promotion of that which the whole policy of the two nations is calculated tf prevent.

Then my right hon. friend comes along with an imitative instinct, which I am glad my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's condemns-my right hon. friend does not admit that he is imitating the States, and I accept his disavowal; but the speech of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) was based almost entirely on the States example-my right hon. friend comes along and he says, "We want some men on the other side of this wall,"-fishermen so to speak-"who will cast their lines over this double wall and endeavour to scoop a little water over it." That is the proposal reduced to the bald economics ' of my right hon. friend. Of course, the States have their men here who are trying to scoop over some of this water also because each Government believes it is quite right for trade to go all one way. But if they would let that trade alone it would flow each way freely.
I have been struggling with the psychology of this matter until my brain is absolutely bewildered. I cannot understand, if the desire be to promote the flow of this water each way, why we put up a dam to prevent its natural flow. Just think of the absurdity of it. We are proposing to have men in the States to scoop this water into Canada and at. the same time my right hon. friend has a colleague who is actually persuading the people on this side-or trying to persuade them, but utterly failing-not to bring in water from the other side. Well, I leave these absurdities for the silent and peaceful rumination of my right hon. friend. He is a great thinker, and I wish he would think out an explanation of the psychology of protectionists and give it to me. He hopes to be here for some years yet, and w^ fondly hope he may prove to be correct-as to how far his interest may be in this chamber for very long is a more doubtful matter-but I do wish before we part that my right hon. friend would settle this point of the psychology of protectionists and explain it to me, because I confess I am 'bewildered about it.
As to these fees, I am thoroughly in agreement with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. This is represented as something that does not cost the Government anything. Well, nothing costs the Government anything. The Government is the mere agent for spending the money of the people of the country, and the point is, that while it is trying to delude itself by thinking it is getting some agents to work for it and is not paying for

it, nevertheless it is a delusion. The work will be paid for, and paid for exactly as I think has been correctly expounded by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. I am surprised at the minister, when we have been working hard here for a good many months, some of us sticking at it day after day, bringing in this worthless proposition at this period of the session. I do not think my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's has been met for one moment in any contentions he made. This will lead to a demand for positions; it is an extension of the Civil Service which all who are studying it contend is too big already. And the most serious thing about it is not only that it costs money to the consumers on both sides of this imaginary line, but that in the end arrangements of this irritating nature only add further to the obstacles to trade that already exist as my hon. friend from Renfrew has pointed out, in too great numbers. I cannot sec what force there is in the proposal. I cer tainly would not do this because the people in the States were doing it. Nations are always doing things which with progress and enlightenment they come to desert, and if we would only learn from the experience of our fellows and desert them a little sooner, we should profit by doing so. If the desire be to bring about trade with the United States, to promote our sales to the United States, there is only one way to do it, and that is not by putting fresh obstacles in the way of trade, but by taking down some of the obstacles that already exist. I may be mistaken, but I honestly believe that my right hon. friend's proposal is not worth the paper it is printed on. It is true that my native land has consular agents for trade, but there is some sense in their having them *-they deal with all the world, in spite of assertions to the contrary, and if the people of England had the chance of summarily dealing with their present Government they would not condone any of the departures from the traditional fiscal policy of the country. Given a country which puts no artificial obstacles in the way of trade, then anything in the shape of agents to help along trade is logical, easily understood, and does not need to go far to get support. But with our present fiscal policy as it is, this proposal of my right hon. friend does not commend itself to my intelligence,, and I am surprised at the time that is being wasted over it at this stage of the session.

I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that as we

have jettisoned a good many things-not because there is any particular storm prevailing, but because we want to lighten the ship so as to make better time-one of the things that could very well be thrown over is this proposed legislation. I venture to say that none of the supporters of the Government came to my right hon. friend and said to him:	Now, we are getting
close to the end of the session, Sir George; do not forget that resolution and that Bill about those agents in the United States.
I venture to think that my right hon. friend was not troubled very much in that way, and that in this matter he is acting upon his own initiative. The hon. member for Brantford replied to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's by saying that if the consumer pays everything the consumer in the United States who takes goods from Canada pays for the $2.50 on that invoice. Well, is that an answer? Is that any reason why we should have our people pay $2.50 that they need not pay? We are not looking after the consumer in the United States; we are entrusted with the duty of looking after the consumer in Canada. If the people of the United States are anxious to have the detailed statistics that d system of this kind will provide and are willing to pay for it, that is no concern of ours. It is a mistake to increase by any amount, large or small, the burden at present borne by the Canadian consumer. It is all very fine to talk about $2.50 being nothing at all. I have heard hon. members from Ontario say that the price of butter has gone down to 25 cents a pound. Well, $2.50 represents ten pounds of butter at that price, and to the ordinary man ten pounds of butter is more, perhaps, than a week's supply for his family. If sugar has gone down to ten cents' a pound, that represents 25 pounds of sugar. When we put these apparently small amounts into sugar, beef, flour and so on, they are not so insignificant. When my right hon. friend Comes to be supporting a family of nine or ten he will find that $2.50 means something. The memories of hon. gentlemen on this side are not as bad as the right hon. gentleman may think. He says to us tonight: Do not 'be alarmed about this army of officers who are to be appointed in the United States; the appointments will all be made by the Civil Service Commission. Well, ever since the Civil Service Commission was appointed we have been hearing that from the right hon. gentleihan, but a few weeks ago he had to tell us that he had appointed over the heads of the Civil 241i
Service Commission 24,000 men in connection with the taking of the census. He has been cutting it down; he now says it is not that many, but those are the figures that he gave us in the first instance.
Let me tell my hon. friend, so that his argument may at least have one premise that is correct, that we are not employing that many men; we are employing about 12,000.	.
Well, the principle is the same. It is bad enough when cut in two.
It is only half as bad.
Did not my right hon. friend himself say it was 24,000?

Yes; I am taking the exact figures as first announced by my right hon. friend. Now he says it is 12,000; we will stay by that figure. But that means that 12,000 officials are appointed as a matter of patronage by the department of my right hon. friend over the heads of the Civil Service Commission. So that when the right hon. gentleman tells us that we have some protection in that Civil Service Commission we have to believe that it is more fanciful than real. If it takes 12,000 men to look after the census for 9,000,000 people, it will require ten times 12,000 to attend to the trade of 110,000,000. If there is to be any kind of service at all and the necessities of this law are to be met, there will have to be someone in every town, village and hamlet in the country where business is done. Then, all these officials will have to be paid, and the money must come from somewhere. They will be Canadian officials, and they must be paid directly or indirectly by the Canadian people. I, therefore, point out to my right hon. friend that it would be well not to suppose that we on this side are so very simple as to take any comfort in his suggestion that he is not going to make those appointments because the Civil Service Commission may do that.
Just one word more. The Civil Service Act was, perhaps, loose enough before, and there were too many loopholes through which too many ministers could break whenever it suited their purpose to do so. But now that we have in process of making the "Spinney" Bill so-called, it makes this ten thousand times worse than it was before, and the "Spinney" Bill so-called is ready for the purpose of putting through anything and everything that must needs

be put through the mill to suit the purposes of the Government and to meet the demands of patronage. There was in this House at one time an hon. member who had much pleasure in using the word "synchronize" and, perhaps, this resolution synchronizes with the "Spinney" Bill so that when the one goes through the other will be ready to facilitate the appointment of this army of officials.

May I just, for the
benefit of the committee take up the subject from the point of view of the other nations of the world as applied to their operations in Canada?

I am
afraid that that can scarcely be discussed on this resolution.

With all due deference
and respect to the Chair, I promise to keep within the lines of the item before the committee. Until I make a breach in those lines, I hope the Chairman will not check me. In Appendix B to report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the year ended March 31, 1920, published by this Government, there is given "an alphabetical list of foreign countries represented in Canada by consuls, vice-consuls, consular agents, and trade agents, according to the latest information supplied to the Department of External Affairs." it proves, I think, the point that, whatever the people of Canada may think about this service, the people of other civilized countries of the world, who are presumed to know something about trade, many of those countries having vastly larger trade than Canada, have found it beneficial to have consular agents in other countries. This information shows that the following countries have consular agents in Canada: Argentine Republic, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Italy, Japan, Liberia, Mexico, Montenegro, Netherlands, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Portugal, Russia, Czechoslovakia, Switzerland, United States. These foreign nations have at least 275 consuls or consular or trade agents in Canada. If these countries have in Canada such an extended service under the caption of trade officials of various kinds and consular agents for trade and other purposes, surely their experience should be a guide to the Canadian Parliament in the adoption of such a progressive policy as the minister contemplates in the resolution before the committee. I might point out that of

these 275 trade agents of foreign countries in Canada, 92 are from the United States. What are they in Canada for except to benefit in some way the people of the United States? I point out to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that Great Britain alone has in the United States 115 consulai or trade agents; the United States have 1,002 agents in the various countries of the world, and with the experience of these older countries before us, surely the argument is overwhelmingly one way. These countries, with a larger experience than ours have seen the benefit of having trade representatives in the various countries of the civilized world, and unless someone can show that Canada can stand to lose by adapting a similar progressive trade policy at a time when our debt is $2,10 p.m. 000,000,000 over the ordinary debt and the only way of stabilising our exchange is by exportation, on the hon. member's own theory, of goods manufactured in this country to other countries of the world, this is an opportunity to press forward progressively and to expand our trade [DOT] through the very medium which the minister has brought forward to-night.
