In what manner does Great Britain pay her trade agents? In the same manner as the United States or as recommended in this resolution?

Great Britain, being so anxious for trade and realizing that she gets trade through the medium of those agents, sends them out and pays them herself. She sees such advantages through these agents that she says: "Great Britain can afford to do that for the sake of trade." She is equipped for trade in a manner that Canada is not; she has been a trader from time immemorial; she knows the advantages; she puts 115 agents of that kind into the United States, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite say that we should not have one.

I admit that I am one of those who asked that these trade agents be appointed. I must say, however, that at the time that I was trying to convince my right hon. friend, I did not think I was succeeding, and I do not think yet that I succeeded. I do not think that the arguments which I and others put forward in favour of trade agents affected him at all. The arguments that our hon. friends opposite put forward by way of protection did influence him. Apparently,

the suggestion now is: Have trade agents and put on a little more protection under cover, as we got a good deal of it on the Budget debate under cover.
My hon. friend's diagnosis is wrong.

I do not think for a moment that we succeeded in having any effect on the minister; but apparently the arguments of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) and others had an effect, because it gave him an opportunity of slipping in a little extra protection under cover. I still believe that we should have trade agents. I quite agree with my hon. friend on that, but I think we' are safer in following the example of Great Britain and the United States in this matter. It is quite true that there is something a little bit unreasonable about appointing trade agents to increase our trade when we are putting up barriers to prevent trade. We must, however, remember that those barriers have been put up. I should like to speak in answer to the argument of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). These barriers are up and we have to deal with existing conditions. The existing conditions are that governments on both sides have put up barriers, but the people still want to trade. It is quite proper that we should adopt some means to overcome those barriers to the greatest possible extent. Therefore, I am in favour of trade agents to overcome to a certain extent the barriers that are placed on the border by the Government on both sides. I believe those agents would not be so much needed if we had free trade. There again I disagree with my hon. friend from Red Deer with whom I do not often disagree in trade matters. I think that the proper and sensible way is to do away with the trade barriers, but as we cannot have that, I believe that this is the next most sensible way. While it is quite true that the increase in protection does not amount to anything like 2i per cent on the average it will amount to that in some particular cases. I do not know what the average trade invoice amounts to, but assuming it to be $500 this tax will amount to half of 1 per cent, which my hon. friend is adding to the customs tariff. While I approve of the idea of having trade commissioners appointed, I cannot approve of this mode of paying them. I am therefore disposed to vote against the proposal. I believe that this scheme has been adopted for the purpose of increasing our customs tariff and for no other purpose.

The provision in the resolution before us is evidently based upon an entirely wrong assumption. It seems to have been assumed that the home market values in foreign countries had remained the same and had not been affected by the war and by depreciation in exchange rates, and that the Government should get the same amount of duty that it would have received had exchange remained normal the world over.
I also wish to quote from an editorial in to-day's Toronto Globe, covering the same point. It is so pertinent to the proposition under consideration, that I think I cannot do better than read it. The editorial is headed "Imports and Exchange" and reads in part as follows:
The National Council of Importers at once produced evidence proving conclusively that the prices of goods affected by the proposed imitation of the depreciation allowance had advanced enormously, as stated in the currency of the countries of origin, and; that "the greater the depreciation in currency the greater have been the advances in price." Tables were compiled and presented to the Senate Finance Committee showing that if even the proposed full allowance of 66 2-3 per cent for depreciation were allowed goods from Poland would pay 61 times the amount of duty now paid on the prevailing rate of exchange; from Austria, 21 times; Hungary, 17 1-3 Jugo-Slavia, 9J; Germany, 4.88 ; Czecho-Slovakia, 4.75; Rumania, 4; Serbia, 2 J ; and Italy, 1 4-10 times the present rates of duty.
In the case of Czecho-Slovakia, which constituted the most highly industrialized portion of the former Austrian Empire, an increase of almost five fold in the duties would have completely barred out the products of the Bohemian industries, that are slowly struggling to their feet. The Czecho-Slovaks are not "enemies" of the United States or Canada, and never were. They fought in the Austrian armies under compulsion, and whenever opportunity served they revolted and went over to the Allies, sometimes by battalions. When the Senate of the United States learned that the proposal to limit the allowance for currency depreciation would hit the friendly people of Bohemia just about as hard a blow as the unfriendly Germans, the proposed amendment was at once dropped and the system of computing duties at the current rate of exchange on the day of exportation will be continued, not only under the Emergency Tariff, but under the permanent measure now being drafted.
The editorial continues:
The tariff jugglers who framed the Currency Depreciation clause of the Budget may have had their eyes on only two or three lines of goods in which Central Europe competes with existing Canadian industries. To prevent importation of these limited ranges of products they have framed a clause that would bar out every article of commerce from Poland, Austria, Bohemia and Rumania, as well as from Germany. That is a case of protection gone mad. When he sees how his proposal works out Sir Henry Drayton is not likely to press it. His advisers have led him into an untenable position.

This is a clear-cut article, one that completely covers the position which I maintain, and I should like to hear a full explanation as to why this resolution is put forward to-night, and whether it is the intention of the Minister of Finance to press it to a conclusion. If enacted, it will cut out completely all merchandise coming from European countries. The citizens of this country buy many lines of goods from those countries which they cannot get at home, and I cannot see what good purpose will be served by a measure of this kind. It will have such far-reaching consequences that I am sure it cannot have been given mature consideration. It could not have been considered from all its angles or it would not have been proposed. It is quite evident that our sister country to the south of us perceived this mistake and corrected it before it was too late. I trust the Minister of Finance will reconsider his decision in the matter and eliminate this provision from the Bill.
Carried.
No, it is not carried.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I entirely agree with the hon. member that the question is a serious one. It is not only serious for the German, but it is also quite serious for the Canadian. I think, however, my hon. friend will agree that it is hardly wise to discuss this' matter in detail on the resolution. I venture to suggest that it can be more properly discussed in detail when the Bill is in committee, and that discussion may be, and ought to be, had without the slightest prejudice to any hon. gentleman because of the fact that the resolution is allowed to pass without detailed discussion. But there are two sides to the story; there are two sets of witnesses. We, of course, have very many of our own, and we can get exactly the same evidence which the hon. gentleman is referring to from the German importer. We do get certain evidence from independent sources. For example-and I want my hon. friend to note this, because we want to do the right thing [DOT]-the mark, worth nominally 23.8 cents, has fallen to as low as 1.6, or perhaps 1.8 cents, which, I think, was the quotation to-day. The mark is still used as the national currency of Germany, and the German workmen are paid in the mark. The average rate of pay in territories not occupied by the Allies-I should hardly say the average rate, because the figure I am about to give is higher than the average-is now 200

marks a week. We will say that a full generous rate is 200 marks a week, and that gives a return to the German labourer of $7.20. Of course, the effect of selling German products in the Canadian market is to turn them into cents, and instead of bringing the German labourer here in person in competition with the Canadian worker, the sale of his products here indirectly does exactly the same thing. The result is that you have in Canada a situation exactly similar to that which you would have if you had a certain portion of industrial employees working at the rate of $7.20 a week, while many of our own men are paid perhaps as much as that a day. I am not arguing for high wages; I merely state what I think is approximately the case, and I submit it for the consideration of my hon. friend. Then there is another thing which has been established pretty well by independent evidence, and that is that there are two prices. The German Government to-day is following the principles of the German Government in the past, and perhaps is going a little further, in connection with assisting exports, so that there'* is a lower price for exports than the prices that prevail in the home market. Now it is quite true that costs in Germany have gone up, and it is equally true that costs have also gone up in Canada, and gone up pretty considerably. I will try to get an article, if I can, for my hon. friend's information, in which a calculation was made in regard to the Sheffield trades in connection with this very matter of the depreciation of German currency, and the extra costs in Germany as compared with the extra costs in England, pointing out how very far short of the amount of depreciation was the inverse increase in costs. How is it working out here, and what is the reason for it? There is unfortunately a large amount of unemployment at present with us. I have in mind at the moment a factory which last year employed 225 persons, I do not know whether men or women. That factory is now employing only 15, and there is a reason for that: they can get no orders. Their ordinary customers have been circularized that if they are wise they will not buy, and the reason for that advice lies entirely with the question of German importations at the present time. There are two things in regard to which I am quite sure my hon. friend is just as anxious as I am. He is anxious to see that the Canadian workman gets a square deal and that the
factories are not closed; and, on the other hand, he is anxious to see that there should not be such a barrier as would work too severely against the German prices. But I would like to tell my hon. friend in connection with German prices quoted in this country that according to the information furnished me those prices have not the slightest relation to German costs. I am told that the selling prices of the German goods are fixed without regard to German cost, but that they have regard to the cost of Canadian production, and then the German manufacturers make such a cut beneath that cost of production as will prevent the Canadian producer from successfully competing. I admit it is a serious question and one which ought to be very carefully considered. My suggestion is-having given my hon. friend what he asked for, the underlying reasons for this-that, without the slightest prejudice to him or any other hon. gentleman, further discussion should be postponed until the Bill -is considered.

How does the minister expect Roumania to repay the advances made to it when the currency of that country would only be worth about 4 per cent in Canada to-day, and the tax in this case would probably equal 200 per cent on Roumanian goods coming into Canada? This country has loaned money to Roumania and it is now proposed to tax that country beyond any possibility of its paying in goods for the advances. The Minister of Finance knows as well as any person that we are only likely to get payment in goods from Roumania or any other country in like position-that it is a matter of the exchange of goods and not of gold these days. Yet my hon. friend insists on increasing the duty on goods from Roumania, and other countries similarly situated, to the extent of 100 or 200 per cent. When he does that there is very little chance of his getting even the interest from Roumania and other countries on the loans that have been made by Canada to them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman forgets that Roumania is an agricultural country, and that we have somewhat of a surplus of agricultural products in this country at present. In Canada we have not a market for agricultural products. I quite admit it is a matter that must be thought over and worked out carefully.

What about Italy? The exchange is very much against Italy at the present time and it is not so much of an agricultural country. How about Greece, and the other countries that the exchange operates against in Canada at present? We are simply imposing an export tax in the case of countries which we hope to do business with that will prevent goods coming in from them; and it is not good business for Canada, or any other country, to put on a tax that will be absolutely prohibitive. It may harmonize with my hon. friend's idea of protection, but it is a case of protecting the smaller class too much and not sufficiently protecting the consumers of this country. The people who are paying the taxes and have furnished the money to enable these loans to be made want to get that money back, and the only way they can get it back is by importing goods from the debtor countries.

Will
the minister tell us how he arrived at the 50 per cent fixed in the resolution? Was it by an arbitrary method, or did he select that figure because of representations made by commercial bodies?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that would occupy some time and I do not think we should go into details at this stage. We can do that when we are considering the Bill; otherwise we shall have two very long discussions when one ought to be sufficient.

The Finance Minister
may be right in his view, but there are one or two matters I would like to bring to his notice so that they will be before him when he is bringing in his Bill. He stated that the average wage of a German workman was $7.20 per week. That compared with the wage paid in this country would seem alarming, but I submit that $7.20 in Canadian money would purchase a much greater amount of commodities in Germany than it would in this country. I am told that in Poland, which adjoins Germany, the Canadian dollar is worth seven hundred marks, or in other words, that seven marks are only equivalent to one Canadian cent. A somewhat similar condition prevails in Germany. Now this provision is apparently aimed at Germany, but why penalize all Central Europe on Germany's account? There are many countries in Central Europe that were friendly to the Allies during the war, and which are therefore entitled to 
special consideration at our hands. For that reason the United States Government, after considering this very same problem decided to refrain from enacting a law of this kind. It is true, as the minister has stated, that goods are very often sold more cheaply in foreign countries than they are in the country of manufacture, but Canadian manufacturers are not immune from that same fault. Not long ago I heard a lecture by an eminent traveller in a committee room in this building. The member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) presided over that lecture and the member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was also present. The lecturer stated that in the interest of his concern he had travelled all round the globe and I think he said the journey occupied a period of two years. He travelled in the interest of the Canada Cycle and Motor Company, and he claimed that during the entire journey he had only met one live Canadian trade agent. I mention that in passing for the benefit of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who can make inquiry from my hon. friend the chairman on the occasion in question if he has any doubt on the point. The gentleman referred to also volunteered the information, in response to a direct question, that his concern sold its products cheaper in other countries than it did in Canada, so that Canadian manufacturers are evidently in the same boat as their competitors in other countries. The chief reason for pursuing this policy, I presume, is to get foreign trade. The minister has advanced the argument that this resolution is designed to help the unemployed in Canada. Well, in my opinion, if we adopt too many schemes of this kind to help the unemployed we will create a class of artisans and workmen in Canada that will be inclined to lie down on their job instead of getting up and going to it like men and competing with the world as they have done in some cases. They have done it in the manufacture of cream separators in Canada, and they have done it in the manufacture of binder twine. The member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) is aware of that fact as he has one of those industries in his own city, and his claim is that that institution is a success because it is under capable management and that all it needs for complete success is to obtain the free importation of the raw material which it uses. That is proof of what I say, from the high priest of protection, the hon. member for Brantford. Now the Canadian workman must not be encouraged to lie down

on his job. I am afraid that all these schemes for protecting the Canadian workmen and trying to stop unemployment will fail absolutely to produce the result the minister has in mind. He says that German costs are framed with regard to Canadian costs. That is the system followed in manufacturing in all countries-the manufacturers frame their costs with the idea of competition. If it were not for competition it would be impossible to live in any country. Nevertheless if you frame the tariff along the lines suggested in this resolution you will absolutely shut out competition from Central Europe. That would be a mistake even in lines of merchandise that compete with the manufactured products in Canada. But it covers the whole gamut of manufactures, many lines that are not made in this country that Canadians must have, and if you shut them out by a tariff of this kind I am afraid that the minister will fall short of the object he has in view. He has my cordial support, and I can assure him that my action tonight is not with the idea of obstructing this measure or creating trouble for him, but rather to help him and the country generally in regard to the legislation which is passed in this House.

One thing is quite
apparent, that the Government not only have abandoned the promise to revise the -tariff, but are seeking ways and means whereby they can increase the tariff without frankly telling the people so. These resolutions afford evidence of it. It is quite clear that the pupose of this resolution is to increase the tariff. If my hon. friend wanted to accomplish that purpose, why did he not do it in a straight and clear way? Not many days ago in discussing our trade relations with the United States my right hon. friend said-and I thought there was a good deal of force in his argument-that by reason of the easy access between Canada and the United States and the large volume of intercommunication there was no need of trade agents being sent over there. That was the general trend of his argument, while of course he very fairly said he would give consideration to what was said on the other side. Now he comes in with a resolution to increase the difficulty of trading with the United States. It may be but small, but it is an increase in the tariff, and I am afraid we will have to reach the conclusion that that was the real aim of the resolution.
I have no desire to encourage German business, and I would think that no matter
how low the price the people of Canada do not want to buy German goods. I should think that any German trader seeking to sell his goods in this country to-day, no matter what price he wanted, would have difficulty in finding a market. But there are principles involved in this. My right hon. friend has given us quotations to show that the German mark is worth less than one-tenth of its former value, but by this resolution you are going to declare it is worth one-half its former value. Therefore you are giving a fictitious value to the goods and charging a duty on what they are not worth. Even though the German mark is worth really only about two cents, where formerly it was worth 24 cents, nearly all things are adjusted accordingly. The financial world has given its judgment of what is the real value of the German mark, and if the Government undertake to collect duty on the real value as established by the proper financial authorities no one could find any fault. Even that will make the duty very heavy. But as the hon. gentleman has said the German mark is worth really only about two cents, and he is going to value it for customs at twelve cents, his is simply adopting a roundabout way, by creating a fictitious value, of largely increasing the taxation which the people of this country are called upon to bear. I do not think it is sound policy, neither do I think it can be defended.
Will my hon. friend allow me to turn to section 3? There is a sentence there which strikes me as curious. It reads:
and by the added provision that the value for duty of new or unused goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production-
And so on. I do not quite understand what he means by "new or unused goods." Perhaps my hon. friend will tell me.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Shop worn goods. For instance, goods that have remained on the shelves for some time.
They would not be new.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: New or unused goods.
Goods are always new until they are used.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: It often occurs that manufacturers or wholesalers have on hand goods shop worn or out of style, and they seek an opportunity to ship them into Canada and sell them at a reduced rate.

By the laws of Canada they ought to be sold at their fair market value. But in this section it is provided:

that the value for duty of new or unuued goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada, plus a reasonable profit thereon.
We have never had any such standard for customs purposes. What have we to do with the cost of production? We impose a duty on the fair market value of the article. If goods are old and shop worn, they have less value, and naturally the price depreciates. This is entirely a new idea. My hon. friend has no machinery whereby he can ascertain the cost of production. It is another attempt to boost the tariff without letting the people of Canada know what you are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: As we all know, there is a surplus amount of goods in the United States, and manufacturers and wholesalers there are very anxious to dispose of them. They establish in the port of export a value by making a few sales here and there in order, as they suppose, to keep within the dumping law. There are scores of manufacturers and wholesale firms that have on their shelves goods that are shop worn and out of style, and they ship them in here at very much reduced rates, which is not fair to the Canadian producer and wholesaler. The idea is to establish what we consider a fair price for the cost of manufacture of these goods at the time of shipment into Canada, and thus prevent dumping. It is possible for us to establish that cost. This department has its own officers and can establish the cost of manufacture by sending them to various points in the United States to investigate and report.

I do not think my hon. friend now has or ever was intended to have any machinery to inquire into the cost of production. He has machinery to ascertain the fair market value. When my hon. friend says that American, manufacturers or wholesalers have sought to establish a market value by an occasional sale here and there, his officials will tell him that that is a distinct evasion of the law, and unless the sales are bona fide and the real market value is established the dumping law will come into operation. There is abundant machinery to-day to give reasonable protection-if you call it protection-to ascertain the market value. If goods are old and shop worn they are not worth the cost of production, for they have suffered deterioration from various causes. But although goods are old and shop worn, and therefore of inferior value, and con-
[Mr. Fielding.1
sequently would have to be sold anywhere at a very low price, the hon. minister is going to have an inquiry as to the cost of production-goods perhaps made in war time-and is going to insist upon that false value and make the Canadian consumer pay duty thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member for Queen's and Sunbury-

Sunbury is coming
soon.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I know a favourable report will come from Sunbury.
Perhaps so.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: These shop worn goods should not come in in competition with our own Canadian goods. As a matter of fact, we have the machinery there, it has been working in the past, and we have received information from our officers in the United States in reference to the cost of manufacture. We take what the cost of manufacture would be at the time of export from the United States.
How are you going to find it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have our officers there.

The hon. gentlemai
says these goods should not come in. Why: Because they are cheap. That is the whole story. The goods might be sold to the unhappy Canadian consumer at a lower price.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is just the same with German goods.

That is another question. The minister says he is going to impose a still greater duty. I have already discussed that question and do not want to go over it again. But here we have shop worn goods, which whether sold at home or abroad have to be sold at a reduced price. They have not the value they formerly had, but the minister is going to create a false value and make the Canadian consumer pay on it.

In order to arrive at some opinion as to how this clause is going to work out, will the minister take one or two articles with which we are all familiar and tell us how he is going to arrive at the actual cost of production? There is a duty on butter coming into this country of about four cents a pound; the same applies to cheese and other

articles. How is the minister going to arrive at the actual cost of production of goods of that nature?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I was not talking about products of the field; I was referring simply to manufactured articles.
Does this clause not apply to all dutiable articles? Besides, is not butter a manufactured article?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly
butter is a manufactured article, and of course it would apply to butter. I am willing to confess that this discussion has one item of novelty to me, and that is the use of the word "shop-worn." I have no doubt it has something to do with the technical working out of the Customs Act. I could not very well discuss that aspect of the issue. But let us see, now: was it intended that the principle of the dumping clauses should function?
Yes, certainly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The dumping clauses were put in to serve a useful purpose-to prevent a sudden change in selling price to the wholesaler or to the manufacturer here of protected goods brought in at a lower rate than they could be fairly sold for in the foreign market-that, is than they could ordinarily be produced for, plus something on top of the ordinary.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well I do not think my hon. friend will argue that you can for very long continue to sell goods at less than the cost of production. The goods will not continue to be produced very long if there is not a little something over that cost in the shape of profit.
Is that the minister's contention with regard to German goods?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I do not quite catch that point; I think it is rather an inverse question that the hon. gentleman is asking. I am discussing for the moment the improper invasion of the Canadian market and the protection to that market which the dumping clause introduced by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was intended to afford. In normal times that dumping provision served its purpose and served it well. But trade in the United States to-day is no more normal than trade is in Canada. In some parts of that country it is even more abnormal than it is in Canada, and the
result is that from time to time certain stocks are liquidated, and liquidated to some extent in the local market. Three, four, five or six local sales are made, sometimes, as we believe, for the purpose of establishing a local market value which really does not exist. So that in that way the dumping clause of my hon. friend can be evaded. I wonder if it is not a good thing that it should continue to be enforced.
I just want to give my hon. friend an illustration. Three samples of goods were produced before me not long ago in connection with the question of the use of Canadian or English material on the one hand and American material on the other. The goods were ladies' dress wear, and I do not think any hon. gentleman could distinguish a difference between them. The price of one sample was $2.65; the price of another, $2.50 and the price of the third, $1.50-and the third sample was American. A quantity of that material was brought into this country. The manufacturer, of course, wanted to get a repeat order shortly afterwards but he could not buy a yard of it; that $1.50 was well below the American cost of production. It was a clean-out sale, and what good did it do here? There was not a cent taken off the ordinary price of the clothing when it was sold to the public, and you could hardly expect that there would be, because the sale of the material was an adventitious sale; it did not represent real value and could only be supported by one or two, perhaps three or four, temporary sales made in a limited area and for a specific purpose. The sending over here from the American market of a large amount of that material was no benefit to the Canadian public; on the other hand, Canadian factories and Canadian workingmen lost work. That is the sort of thing that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's wanted to stop, and he did stop it. But as I have said, these are not normal times, and the purpose of the resolution, as I understand it, is to provide that the value for duty purposes of such new or unused goods, goods which are not second-hand, shall be thus tested.

I think that the Chairman will be amused when I point out to him the fact that he has been the chairman of a committee on the fuel question which has been endeavouring to ascertain the cost of the production of coal and other fuels in Canada. The committee has been thus engaged for some weeks, and we are

quietly told by the minister now that he has the machinery by which he can determine, in relation to goods which are in a more advanced state of manufacture than coal, the cost of production in the United States.
And in foreign countries.

And tell that in foreign countries. We wanted to get the cost in the United States of this coal that we have been inquiring about, and it is certainly very negligent on the part of that committee that it did not call those officials of the Customs Department to give it that information. That is a simple matter compared with what you are attempting at this time. The other day I stepped into one of the largest stores in Ottawa, and I happened to run across an old acquaintance who is now in charge of purchasing in that store. He showed me piece of goods after piece of goods which were selling a short time ago at from $7 to $11 a yard. They are selling the same goods to-day for $3, $3.50 and $4 a yard, and he told me that they were making more money on them now than they did when they were selling them at from $7 to $11 per yard. That just illustrates the condition of trade with which you are endeavouring to deal at the present time. Values are going down, are changing, because of the change in the cost of raw materials, and I think, Mr. Minister of Customs, you will have to have a very much more extensive staff than you have yet persuaded this side of the House, at least, that you have the command of, to keep in touch with that and not to work unjustly to the genuine importer of such goods.
While I am on my feet, I want also to comment on the next clause which has to do with this 50 per cent on exchange. I have just secured the latest quotations with regard to Italian exchange. At par it should be 19.3 cents for the lira. It is now 6.24 cents. Therefore, you would put a value of 9.6 or 9.7 cents on goods that have cost 6.24 cents; you will rate your customs upon the higher value, and the consequence is that, with a 20 per cent customs tariff, you have a 75 to 80 per cent duty. In the present state of trade, when there is a possibility that we shall not be able to sell to the United States in the measure that we have sold to that country in the past, due to their unfriendly, if I may so call it, customs, we want to find other markets, and if we find markets to sell in, 
we have to take goods back. One of those prospective markets is Italy. Our trade in the past with that country may not have been very great, but this measure is distinctly designed to kill that trade. We cannot take goods from them; they cannot afford to sell us goods on which we have to pay a duty of 75 or 80 per cent, and that is what this means. When I spoke on this question the other day, I was somewhat concerned as regards France and Belgium whom I felt we should not turn our sword against at this time. With the German indemnity, their exchange is up around 9.77 cents, which is just 11 p.m. over the half way mark, so that they will probably not be touched, because I think, with the continuance of the payment of that indemnity, their condition will be improved, and they will be out of reach of this most unfriendly measure. But with regard to Italy and other European countries, to which, it will be understood, we must look for increasing markets for our produce, you are going to make it impossible for them to exchange goods with us.

I regret the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has formed quite a misconception as to the purpose of the dumping duty. He is labouring under the delusion that the dumping duty was designed to prevent the people of Canada from getting cheap goods. It was not designed to do anything of the sort. Those who brought about the dumping duty were perfectly willing that the people of Canada should get cheap goods, provided that that cheapness was the cheapness of the market generally. What was the condition that the dumping duty was intended to meet? There are notable cases which arise in my mind now where an American manufacturer, having a large quantity of goods which he desired to sell, was prepared to sell in Canada at a lower price than he sold at home. Our complaint was not that he sold the goods cheaply. As long as he charged the Canadian buyer the same price as he charged his home buyer, there was no dumping. But when he created a fictitious price, where he charged one dollar in the United States and offered to sell the same goods for 75 or 80 cents in Canada, we felt that that was not a legitimate transaction, and it was to meet that sort of thing that the dumping clause was designed. As long as there is created for the Canadian market a price which is not the real price at home, the dumping clause comes in.

It provides an ample duty; the machinery is in the hands of the Minister of Customs, and there is no need of anything more. When my hon. friend repeated the argument that special sales are made to establish a price, I say, without a moment's hesitation, that the Customs Department is not bound to accept and it will not accept those sales. In the earlier days of the dumping duty, there were some difficulties. It was described by an eminent English statesman as a piece of freak legislation. As time went on and the efficient officials of the department got a good grasp of the question, the thing worked out quite well. The only thing to be determined is: Is this a fair price as quoted in the home market? The design was not to prevent the people of Canada from getting cheap goods. If an article is made cheap on account of a surplus in the market, or by changing conditions, or if raw material is cheaper, or if one of the hundred and one things that enter into the cost of production is cheapened and the article is thus made cheaper, and it is as cheap in Canada as in the United States, there is no reason in the world why we should impose any barriers to keep it out. The real purpose of this proposed legislation is to create a fictitious price in order that you may increase the duty, which many people think is high enough already, but which, in some instances, would be made double what it would otherwise be.

I think the impression that we had in Canada of the dumping clause was that it was to prevent Americans from shipping goods in here under the price at which those goods were sold in the United States. When the dumping clause was in force under the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), I know from experience in general as regards machinery, canning machinery, for instance, which is expensive and which we use a great quantity of, the price, when the machinery came to the border, has been raised under our Canadian dumping clause from $600 to $1,000, and we have had to pay duty on that for any number of machines running into quite a large amount of money. That was what the dumping clause did for us. I think we all agree as regards the purpose of it, and I do not see much difference between that and the present legislation. We must not forget what the Americans did as regards, us. I have had experience in regard to shipping goods into the United States, and they have all this machinery for which the minister
is now trying to provide. It is said by speakers on the other side that it is impossible to carry out this legislation, to get at the values and to assess the duty. The people of the United States are doing it; they have no difficulty at all in doing it; they assess the value, and they hold up the goods until they get the value.

Does the
hon. member mean "value" or "cost of production"?
I mean value.
That is different.

They get at the value and the cost of production. I have in my possession a letter from a firm in Canada which has 50 cases of a certain line of goods lying at Black Rock. They are trying to get them into New York, having sold them there. These goods have been held at that point for nearly three months. The United States authorities have given no reason at all why they should not go through. The goods are properly valued, but they raise every objection and every obstacle they possibly can. Let me give an instance. A year or perhaps two years ago a branch factory that we have in the United States wanted to get something that we had in Canada, which we had imported from England and which they could not get at that time in the United States. They asked us to send over a certain quantity and we sent a thousand pounds of these goods to our own factory in Buffalo. The United States sent an appraiser from Washington to examine our books and go over our invoices in our home town at Dunnville. The officers reported that everything was fair and square, and they did not see why there should be any difficulty at all, but in th: face of that report those goods were held in Buffalo, and we were fined $1,200 for undervaluation. There was no undervaluation at all. We had bought the goods in England, and we added to them the freight and took advantage of the exchange for profit. I even referred the matter to Ottawa to see if they could not investigate this awful imposition of a fine of $1,200, but they reported that it was according to the American law and that there was no use talking about it. You have to show a profit of 10 per cent on your goodi or you cannot pass them. That is the way they treat us. Surely we are not going to treat them as generously as some hon. gentlemen would have us do. The values are raised and everything is done to prevent you shipping to the United States.

It is not a question of how we should treat the American shipper but of how we should treat the Canadian consumer. We are not concerned if the American Government acts foolishly. It is not for us to follow their example. Their method may he good or it may be bad, but if that is the result of the determination of the American people to do business in this way the scheme we have been discussing on this resolution of sending over there a lot of trade agents to sell our goods would be a waste of money. But we are not concerned about the American people. We are concerned about the people of Canada who are going to pay this tax and who are going to be made to pay an extortionate duty which is not boldly mentioned in the tariff but is brought about in this round about way.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In reply to my hon.
friend from Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy) there is no question of valuing the cost of production of butter or cheese; it is so much per pound, not on the cost of production at all.

I propose to demonstrate
that this clause by which no reduction shall be allowed in excess of 50 per cent of the value of the standard or proclaimed currency of the country from whence the goods are invoiced to Canada will have the effect in some cases of raising the duty 500 per cent.
I take the Weekly Bulletin of April 25, 1921, published by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I find that on April 20 -this is not quite up to date, but there is no difference between the quotation of th^t day and the quotation of to-day-the German mark, which has a parity value of 19.8 cents had a value of 1.72 cents; that the Italian lira which has a parity value of 19.3 cents, had on that date a value of 5.45 cents, and that the Roumanian lei, which has a parity value of 19.3 cents, the same as the franc and the lira, had on that day the value of 1.81 cents.
Now, to prove my assertion, I will take the actual value of the German mark and the actual value of the Roumanian lei, which are about the same. Suppose that certain goods were bought in Roumania and sent to Canada, and that they had a valuation of 100 lei in Roumanian money. In Canadian money these goods would have a value of $1.81. If the duty on these goods was 25 per cent, it would amount to 45 cents. Now, if we take into consideration the fact that in order to give currency one-

half its nominal value we have to multiply it by five, it means that we have to take five lei at the present time to be equal to a lei in ordinary times. Therefore, if I multiply this duty of 45 cents on 100 lei of merchandise by five, the duty that will be paid on these goods will be $2.25, or five times more than the duty that would be charged if the actual cost of these goods was taken into account; in other words, a duty of 500 per cent more than the ordinary duty. The effect of this provision will be to close entirely this market to Germany, to Roumania, and to Italy, unless double the duty is paid on Italian goods. As was stated quite correctly a few moments ago by an hon. gentleman on this side of the House, France will not be barred from this market, because the French franc is about half its parity value now. But the other countries which I have just mentioned, which are in a position to sell goods cheaply to the Canadian consumer, will be debarred from doing so- by the duty which is absolutely prohibitive.
I find in this scheme an indirect, or perhaps a direct, way of raising the duties on goods. When the' tariff duties were discussed and drafted, we took into account the fact that the goods were to be valued, not according to the standard of Canadian money, but according to the price at the place where they were bought. By this stratagem in the resolution before us we are simply raising the customs duties all the way from 100 to 500 per cent. Therefore, the consumer will have to pay as high as 500 per cent more duty on goods coming from the countries I have just mentioned than he would have to pay if this proposal was not accepted.
I think I have said enough to demonstrate that this is simply a method of raising the duty on goods coming from certain countries, the duties on these goods, of course, having to be paid by the Canadian consumer. We are altogether losing sight of the fact that the poor people of this country are still laburing under the burden of the high cost of living. The only way at present of reducing the cost of living is to admit such goods as I have mentioned, but by raising the customs duties some 500 per cent, by the method that has been explained, these goods will certainly be kept out of Canada, and the Canadian consumer will not be able to obtain his requirements at reasonable price?

The member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), asked a question

to which I also should like to have an answer, and that is as to how the Govk ernment arrived at 50 per cent as a fair basis to start on. I am entirely opposed to the principle of this section, and I want some explanation as to how this 50 per cent has been arrived at.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is a matter of
exchange which the Minister of Finance can better deal with.

Where is the Minister of
Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: He is on the other side at present.

Perhaps the Minister
of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), will oblige us with an explanation.

Let something
stand for discussion when the Bill is under consideration.
I am opposed to the principle of the resolution, and if we allow the resolution to pass, we adopt the principle.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In arriving
at these figures one can only approximate. There are many different statements as to how costs have gone up in Germany. It is stated that owing to the low standard of living of the German worker to-day, the cost of production has not very materially increased there. The hon. member is conversant with the details of the steel business. German pig iron can be produced and put on the export market at 500 marks a ton, and that shows a very slight increase in the actual cost of manufacturing. The hon. member will also realize that the relation between increased cost on the one hand and depreciation of currency on the other is a material question, and we should also bear in mind what has happened to our own currency. The arguments which hon. gentlemen opposite have made in connection with the loss of buying power of the Canadian dollar have also to be considered. If those arguments are at all right, it is hardly fair that the German mark should be taken at the lowest possible standard and the Canadian dollar held up to practically its pre-war basis. It is therefore difficult to arrive at anything like a scientific basis, and I think we should probably discuss the question to better advantage when we are in committee on the Bill, when we should be able to see what modifications or extensions ought to be made. It may be that something should be done in connection with other considerations not yet fully
covered, as for instance, the question in regard to Czecho-Slovakia already mentioned.

Is it not the intention of the Government practically to prohibit importations from certain countries? That is undoubtedly what the minister has in mind. Well, why penalize other countries? Personally I would not penalize Germany any more than Greece, Roumania, Belgium, France or England. We. went through the process of adopting and signing the treaty, and were told that we were at peace with the Central Powers, and if it is the intention now to penalize them to the extent of prohibiting their goods, we had better de-clare'that we are still at war. If this does not mean that we intend to penalize these people, then it must be our intention to penalize the Canadian people. If the Canadian cannot buy his goods where he wants to and pay the duty on them, you are merely adding to the cost which the consumer has to pay; or you are attempting to prohibit importations entirely. Let us understand just what is the intention.
I understood from the Minister of Customs (Mr. Wigmore), when he introduced the resolution, that it had virtually been in effect since 1918 through Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
What I said had no
reference to this resolution; I referred to the amalgamation of the two departments.

It seems to me that my hon. friend would have made much more rapid progress with his resolution if he had given to the committee the information that was given by hon. gentlemen on the other side. I was very much impressed with the arguments made by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Boys), and my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon), in regard

to certain matters on this resolution. What I contend is that the Minister of Customs and Excise has not given a sufficient and proper answer to the arguments adduced by hon. gentlemen opposite who took up time this afternoon, as they had a perfect right to do, in bringing these matters to his attention. For example, in answer to the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), who is not now in his seat, as to what occurred by reason of the operation of the present law and the necessity for its amendment so as to provide relief in cases of hardship-a matter which arose in connection with section 7-the minister replied that his officers had been. overefficient.
He said over-officious, not over-efficient.

I accept the correction. But if the minister said his officials were overofficious I would take that to be a criticism of them. On account of that over-offieious-ness the minister said the department had shown leniency in regard to the special case brought to his attention. One would naturally suppose from that statement that the fine imposed had been remitted by the department, but when the question was put to him by my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) as to whether the fine had been collected he said it had been. Now if such defects as these are shown in the operation of the law, now is the time to correct them and not wait until we have approved of the principle of the resolution. If we do make the amendments now, we will be told when the Bill founded upon the resolution is introduced " Oh this is only carrying out the resolution as it passed the committee." Then my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Boys) raised the question as to what this resolution really means. Now it seems to me that the minister seeing that he has his officials around him, and had time, during the recess from six to eight o'clock, to confer with them, ought to be able to tell the committee what the resolution really does mean and what its affect will be in the carrying on of business throughout the country. No person wants to interfere in any way with the passage of this resolution, or of the Bill to be founded upon it, if the legislation proposed is really in the interests of the country. But he is very reticent in the explanations he has been giving not only to hon. gentlemen on this side but to hon. members around him as well-in fact most of the criticisms of the department, and

of the resolution my hon. friend is moving, came from hon. gentlemen opposite in the early part of the discussion this afternoon. It ought to be easily possible to give full information touching the first clause of the resolution which has been in operation I understand for upwards of two years. Besides suggesting to my hon. friend that he should make some general statement in regard to the meaning and affect of the other clauses of the resolution, I would ask him to explain how the changes made by Order in Council in 1918 have worked out. Has there been a saving to the country by the amalgamation of the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue which are henceforth to be known as the Department of Customs and Excise? I would like him to explain how the amalgamation has worked out in particular localities, whether it has been found to be an advantage or a disadvantage. For example in the city of St. John has the amalgamation of the two departments resulted in a saving or has it involved additional expenditure? Then I would like to know what the affect has been in other parts of the province of New Brunswick, how it has operated throughout the country generally? It seems to me the committee would, like to have a frank and open statement from the minister in regard to all these matters. It he had done that earlier in the discussion we might have got along very much more rapidly than we have been doing but we have been obliged to draw out explanations in regard to every little item in every clause-practically as regards every sentence almost in each clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I thought I had already given considerable information to the committee. Clause 7 of the resolution provides:
That section one hundred and eighty of the said Act be amended to provide that the certificate of a provincial analyst shall be accepted as evidence Off the alcoholic content of the beer or wash suitable for the manufacture of spirits.
Out of that arose the discussion of section 180 of the Act dealing with stills, and so forth, which I read to the committee this afternoon. What is now proposed does not change the section in question. It merely contemplates the appointment of an analyst. Formerly an analysis could only be made by the officers of our department. What we now want to do is to have that analysis made by a provincial officer or an officer of the Health Department. This section has been on the Statute Book for thirty-five years and that is the

only change that is now proposed to be made with respect to it.
As far as the amalgamation of the two departments is concerned it has been operating satisfactorily for the last year, the Civil Service Commission, under the guidance of the Re-organization Committee suggesting certain changes in each department in Ottawa and in the Outside Service as well. Certain recommendations have been made by this committee on re-organization and to some extent those recommendations have been carried out. My hon. friend from Westmoreland has spoken of the affect of the amalgamation in the city of St. John. Well, certain reductions in the staff have been made there, and greater reductions will be made in the future, but the work is being performed under the reduced staff resulting from amalgamation as efficiently as it was carried on by the former larger staff. Now as to other cities. In Montreal the Customs Department was established in a building in one section of the city, and the Inland Revenue Department in another building in another section of the city. The two departments have been brought together in the one building, and certain reductions of the staff have taken place there. The same applies to Toronto. From reports that we have received not only from our officers but from outside, it is apparent that the work is being carried on to the greater satisfaction of the public generally. We will effect quite a saving by the amalgamation. It is a pleasure for me to accommodate hon. gentlemen, and if I can furnish any further information I shall be happy to do so.

What is the policy of the Government when the two departments are amalgamated? Does the Civil Service Commission make the change? A case was brought to my attention at St. Hyacinthe, where , Dr. A. P. Cartier had been the collector of inland revenue for seven years, and M. Handihan, collector of customs. Dr. Cartier was the younger man, had always given good service, and was perfectly fitted for the position, but now by this change he loses his position. What is the policy of the Government regarding these matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
All these changes are made on the recommendation of the reorganization committee to a sub-committee of council. In that particular case the collector of customs was also made collector of inland revenue, and it was therefore
necessary to dispense with the services of the other man.

Who are the
parties forming the reorganization committee?

This discussion might be proper when the Estimates of Civil Government in connection with the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue are before the committee, but on this resolution it is quite out of order.

I would like to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but the minister has just given the policy of the Government regarding the amalgamation of the two departments, and he invited members to put questions. I am sorry to understand that the chairman of the committee and the minister differ.

Order. The Chairman has given his ruling, which is not debatable. Apart from that, the fact that the minister invited questions, does not make the discussion in order.
Shall the resolution carry?
No.
Will the minister tell us the personnel of the reorganization committee that he has spoken of?
I hope it is not necessary for me to repeat my ruling.

I respect your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but the minister has just spoken about the reorganization committee. I submit that it is perfectly in order to ask him who are the parties forming that reorganization committee. It is a very simple question that it might be in the interests of the people to answer.

Mr. Chairman, we shall have items before the committee on which that question will come up and be thoroughly discussed. Would it not be well for my hon. friend to leave this extraneous matter until then?
Two words will satisfy me.
He might be away when the question comes up.
Oh, no, he is going to stay here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. R. W. WIGMORE (Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 211 respecting the Department of Customs and Excise.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) Bill No. 139 to amend the Immigration Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-non-immigrant classes:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would suggest that we consider this section clause by clause. I know some members-not present to-night -are interested in certain clauses of this Bill and wish to make representations in regard to them, and I think, even if the clauses are passed, it might be on the understanding that any hon. gentlemen who desire to raise any question in regard to them shall have the privilege of doing so later. With regard to the first proposed amendment, I may say that under the law two classes of persons are defined, immigrants and non-immigrants. Immigrants must go through a certain procedure which is not required of nonimmigrants. Among the non-immigrant classes there are included the following: members of dramatic, artistic, athletic or spectacular organizations entering Canada temporarily for the purpose of giving public performances or exhibitions of an entertaining or instructive nature, and actors, artists, lecturers, priests and ministers of religion, authors, lawyers, physicians, professors of colleges and commercial travellers entering Canada for the temporary exercise of their respective callings. During the last two or three years the international trade unions have made representations that their accredited representatives who are required to come to Canada from time to time should be included in the description of non-immigrant classes, and there is no reason why they should not be so enumerated in this section. As to the second proposed amendment, under the law as it now stands there must be an officer at a place before it can be designated as a port of entry. It is proposed that a port of entry shall be any place so designated by the minister. The change is a very simple one, purely for administrative purposes.
How many ports of entry are there now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should say seventy, probably eighty.
Is it the intention to add to this number?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. It may be found necessary to designate a place temporarily as a port of entry. It is not for the purpose of increasing the number of the ports of entry.

Has the Government
any control over a person who enters this country from Europe and shortly after reaching Canada goes to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, we cannot prevent that. The third amendment is to paragraph (q) of section 2. The term "enter Canada" is applied throughout the law to non-immigrants and "land in Canada" to immigrants. A number of amendments are included in the Bill, some for the purpose of including the terms "enter" and "or land in," which happened to have been left out when the consolidation took place some two years ago. Here it is proposed to insert in paragraph (q) the words "or land in" in order to cover the two classes. The fourth amendment merely inserts the words "passengers or other persons" in the definition of "immigrant station." The law as it stands refers only to immigrants.

Might I suggest to my hon. friend that he give instructions to certain immigration officials who are a little too fussy? We had a very striking example the other day when a distinguished visitor to Canada and his wife were subjected to very severe treatment on the part of the immigration officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am having some difficulty along that line more or less all the time. I am sure the hon. gentleman can understand that these officers are very anxious to carry out the law. Sometimes', though, they may use bad judgment and, in the exercise of their discretion, not do just the right thing. Whenever any matter of that kind comes to my attention I always communicate with them with the object of having the law sanely and reasonably administered, as it should be.
My hon. friend knows to what I refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Sectjon agreed to.

On section 2-Board of Inquiry:
What are the powers of the board of inquiry contemplated in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They have power to prevent the entry or landing of either an immigrant or a non-immigrant.
Subject to appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-hearing of cases:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Previously this referred to "such" board. Now, you may have two or three boards at any one port. Therefore, we are inserting the word "a" in place of the word "such", so as to cover all boards that may be carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 5 agreed to.
On section 6-costs of appeal to be paid by unsuccessful appellant.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Under the law as it now stands, if a person is rejected by a board of inquiry, that person is required to make a deposit of $20 for himself, and if he has any dependants with him, $10 for each dependant, in order to pay for the cost of his maintenance during such time as the appeal is pending. We propose that, in addition to his paying for the cost of his maintenance, we should include the costs or expenses of the appeal. Supposing a person comes from some Eu-12 m. ropean country; he lands at Quebec; our officers there decide that he should be rejected because he does not comply with the law. Immediately he and his friends get busy and they want action taken very quickly. This means a great deal of telegraphing and telephoning, and the aggregate cost of this to the department amounts to a very large sum. It is desirable on the other hand that there should be quick action from the standpoint both of the department and of the party concerned. Our officers think it is only fair in those cases where it has been decided to hold up an intending immigrant, that the immigrant himself, if he has been rejected by a board of inquiry, should pay the cost of telegraphic and telephonic communication. To the individual the cost may not mean very much, but during the year the cost to the country runs into thousands of dollars. The purpose of this amendment is simply to require that an immigrant who
242i
has been rejected and who appeals should pay the cost of those communications.
What happens if the man is of very limited means and is not able to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If he has not the money, I presume we would have to pay for this.

My hon. friend speaks of large costs. I cannot see how the cost should be so very large. Of course, during the time which elapse between the appeal and the decision of the department, the man has to pay for his maintenance. Let us say that in immigrant lands at Quebec to-day; he is rejected, and he has to remain, say eight days in Quebec before taking the boat or having a decision on the appeal lodged with the department. What is the average cost for maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The cost of his actual maintenance would be comparatively small. In the contract which we have just let at Quebec for catering, the successful caterer has agreed to give three meals for 75 Gents.
Are there costs for the forms to be filled in?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Only the long distance telephoning and telegraphing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is all. Supposing a man comes from Great Britain and some questions are raised as to his right of entry into Canada. Very frequently we have to cable two or three times before we get the required information. Sometimes, half a dozen communications will be sent out to some place in British Columbia in order to get quickly exact information as to a man's right to be in Canada. The cost of all this to the individual may be comparatively small, but I can assure the-committee that it runs into many thousands of dollars for the department-
Supposing the immigrant does not speak either English or French. Will he have to pay the cost of an interpreter?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-powers of board exercised by officer in charge:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The law, as it now stands reads that where there is no board of inquiry at a port of entry or at a neighbouring port to which a person detained .under this Act could conveniently be, con-

veyed or to which a case for decision could be conveniently referred, then the officer in charge shall exercise the power. We are cutting out that portion of the clause that relates to a board of inquiry at some other place nearby. It has landed the department in all sorts of trouble, and under that clause as it stood, we have lost one or two cases under habeas corpus proceedings.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8

bill of health.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Clause 8 provides that the form of the bill of health shall be approved by the minister. The present law does not state how that form of the bill of health is arranged for.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-medical examination:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Under the law as it
stands, this clause reads: "medical officers appointed under this Act." They are not appointed under this Act now; they are appointed under the Department of Health Act, and, therefore, the words "appointed under this Act" are struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-landing of passengers:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are no radical
changes. The first amendment is that section 33, subsection 1, is struck out and a new clause substituted. The only change in that is as follows: The law as it stood stated that:
Every passenger or other person seeking to enter or land in Canada shall first appear before an Immigration officer-
That is changed to read:
-shall first appear and make application to an immigration officer at a port of entry-
The words "at a port of entry" are inserted. He shall make application at a port of entry. That is the spirit of the whole law:
-for permission to enter or land in Canada-
We put in both expression again.
-and shall be detained for examination-
As the section reads now:
He shall be forthwith examined as required under this Act.
Then the clause goes on:

which shall be conducted forthwith on shipboard or on train, or at some other place designated for that purpose.

This is simply to make the present lav, a little clearer.
The second amendment is an addition to subsection 2, and it is a rather important one. It provides a penalty for answering questions falsely. We have officers, say at Niagara or Windsor or Quebec or Halifax, and these immigrants are coming in and they are required to answer questions. They are coming in from the United States on the train in the second or third class car, and our officer goes through and asks certain questions. Their answers are taken down. Of course, the officers have not time to take an affidavit from every man or anything of that sort. Now the proposal is that if these questions are not answered truthfully a penalty follows.

On that very point, I have had occasion before to call the attention of the minister to a situation that has existed to my own knowledge where officers have been putting questions in English to persons speaking only the French language and coming to a country where both languages are official. With the law as it is now drafted, I presume the same situation will continue to exist, and that immigrants from Belgium and France will be submitted to the same trouble that immigrants from those countries have had in the past, of having no one on the boats or on the trains to put the questions in French. That is the situation now, it was the situation a year ago, and in the years before that. The hon. minister promised a year ago that he would remedy this situation, but he has not done so. He comes here now with a new Bill, leaving the situation just as it was before. I would like him to give a little attention to this very important matter. Desirable immigrants from France and Belgium are put to all kinds of trouble due to the immigrant officers not being able to put their questions in the French language.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will have to get the matter straightened out.
How will it be done?
Where in this Bill will you put the few words that are necessary to make it law?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not necessary to have it in the law.
It is better to have it in the law. Ministers may change.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The third amendment
[DOT] inserts only the words "enter or" in one

part. There is also a contradiction between subsections six and seven of the present law. Subsection six provides:
Every person who enters Canada except at a port of entry shall forthwith report such entry to the nearest immigration officer,
and so on, while the very next subsection provides:
Any person who enters Canada except at a port of entry. .	.	. shall be guilty of an
offence.
The two subsections are contradictory. It is proposed to change subsection six to read:
It shall be a violation of this Act for any person to enter Canada except at a port of entry.
The section will then be in conformity with all the other sections of the law.
Suppose the person is an actor or an athlete who does not come through a port of entry, but may be travelling on the high road. Would this apply to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The law reads that it shall be a violation "for any person to enter Canada except at a port of entry". It would not make any difference whether he was an actor or an athlete. If he does not come in through a port of entry, he is violating the law as it now stands. That is the provision that runs all through the Act.
Then subsection 9 is changed slightly. This clause provides a penalty for transportation companies or persons interfering with the immigration officers in the discharge of their duties. The law now reads: "Any transportation company or person interfering with or resisting." We are inserting after "company" the words "director, official or employee thereof, or any person interfering with," and so on. Then further down in the subsection it says: "assisting in the escape of any person detained." We are putting in after "detained" the words "in the custody of an officer." The only real difference between the law as it stands and this amendment is that we are including the officers of transportation companies or any other person that interferes with an immigration officer in the discharge of his duties. Then the words "entry or" are inserted before "landing".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-immigrants may be required to possess prescribed amount of money:
I understood that each male immigrant was required to have $250. This section provides that the amount may vary "according to the nationality, race, occupation, or destination of such persons."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are making only a very slight change in the existing law. Under the existing law we may make regulations fixing whatever amount may be deemed advisable. For the present that amount is fixed at $250 except in the case of farmers, farm labourers, domestics and so on.

Is that the maximum
or the minimum?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Is there any question of religion?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. These are the only
