two changes in the first part of the law. In the last part, provision is added to the effect that passports shall not be recognized unless issued within a time limited by the regulations, or unless vised in the manner required.

The minister gave me information in regard to farm labourers from the British Isles, who he said were not required to meet the money qualification. Does that statement apply to farm labourers from other countries, say, for example, Austria?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, unless they come
within the prohibited classes.

That is to say, alien
enemies, like Germans?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
I ask the question because I have had some inquiries on the subject.

Apart from former
enemy immigrants, is there any policy of discrimination in the department against certain countries, such as Spain, for instance, or southern Italy? Is there a bar to immigrants coming from those countries? I understand that the department does not encourage immigration from the southern portions of Europe, but I suppose it is within its discretion, whenever a proper immigrant comes from those countries, to admit him?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right; there is no bar. We may not encourage immigration from those parts, but if an immigrant is mentally and physically desirable, and has the necessary money prescribed he is not rejected.
Does the minister think he will have to enforce the clause with regard to the money qualification so far as tourists are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I doubt it, as regards tourists. The non-immigrant class is very wide, and includes a very large number of people. I am advised by the officials of our department that we have had a number of cases where people have come in under that guise and have become public charges on the community, and it may be advisable as regards some of them to require the money qualification.
Were these people generally Americans, or were they from overseas?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know.
Because, if the minister starts to require the money qualification from American tourists, he will discourage a great many Americans from coming here.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will not do that.
The matter is left wholly in the discretion of the immigration officers at the different ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Suppose a tourist wanted to enter Canada, would he have to satisfy the local immigration officer as to his fitness, and so forth, if he comes within that class? Any such wide power given an officer of the department seems to me to be dangerous.
[Mr. Calder.J

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I entirely agree with
that, and I have very much doubt as to whether this provision would apply very largely to tourists. As I pointed out, these classes of people are non-immigrants, such as members of dramatic, artistic, athletic, or spectacular organizations entering Canada temporarily for the purpose of giving performances or exhibitions, and actors, lecturers, priests, and ministers of religion, authors, lawyers, professors of colleges, and commercial travellers. These are all non-immigrants. I dare say what the department is aiming at is the control of the strolling circuses and bands of that kind coming for the purpose of giving exhibitions. Many of them become public charges in Canada.

Travelling in Europe a year ago I found that the authorities there were just as drastic in their restrictions as we are in Canada. For instance, passing from Dover to Boulogne or Calais, or from the Italian boundary to French territory, you have to sign many official documents, and sometimes show your purse to prove that you have the necessary amount exacted by the authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We do not yet know what inconvenience means in this country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-investigation of complaints-deportation-cost of deportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is the section that was included in the Bill last year introduced, although not passed, in the Senate, and reintroduced in this House by the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Two years ago, a clause was inserted in the Immigration law dealing with persons guilty of sedition, and provision was made for their deportation. It is proposed to repeal a portion of the section in the law as it now stands. The section at present provides that it shall not apply to any person who is a British subject either by reason of birth in Canada or naturalization in Canada. It is proposed to amend it so as to read that the section shall not apply to any Canadian citizen. There is a wide difference between the two. "Any Canadian citizen" would include a person who came to Canada from the British Isles, was here for a short time, and acquired domicile in Canada. The old law did not provide for that. If a person came from the British Isles and acquired domicile here, say four or five months, he would be

subject to deportation under the old law. He is not, under this amendment.
That is, the amendment moved by the member for Quebec East.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. Then it is proposed that subsection 2 of said section should be repealed as it is retroactive in its character.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-cost of deportation after five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is simply using the words "any person" instead of the word "immigrant." That is it includes non-immigrants as well as immigrants.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-form e amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is merely to carry out a provision that was not corrected two years ago when the law was amended. It is in one of the forms.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-form ee amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is for the same purpose; it is merely amending a form that was not amended a few years ago. I propose to leave the Bill in committee because some hon. members who are not here to-night are interested in it. I would therefore move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Calder Bill No. 146 to Amend the Chinese Immigration Act was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-all immigrants must establish identity to satisfaction of controller subject to approval of minister.
Please explain this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reading of the section will explain nothing at all unless the members of the committee have the Statute before them. Under section 7 of the law as it stands, persons of Chinese origin entering Canada are required to pay a head tax of $500 unless they belong to what is called "the exempt classes." Paragraphs a, b and c, of this section set out the exempt classes:-members of the diplomatic corps and other proper representatives, children born in Canada of parents of
Chinese origin who leave this country tor educational purposes, and so on. Then paragraph c includes merchants, their wives and minor children; clergymen, tourists, men of science, teachers, clergymen and students. Now in so far as these exempt classes are concerned they become exempt if they substantiate their status to the Controller of Chinese Immigration, or if they produce certificates of identity issued by the proper officers of the Chinese Government. These certificates of identity must also be countersigned by British consular officers or other representatives of His Majesty's Government in China. To be quite frank, during the course of the last two years, particularly this last year-very largely on account of conditions existing in China, because they have not stable Government in the whole of China-the administration of the law nas fallen down very badly in connection with these certificates of identity.
Canton.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. We had a good deal of trouble during last year, and a very large number of these people got into Canada under these certificates who should never have entered the country. After going into the matter very fully, we have come to the conclusion that, for the time being at any rate, the only thing to do is to repeal that clause and simply provide that when these people come forward seeking to enter Canada they must substantiate their status as men of science, or as teachers, or as students, or as merchants, to our Controller of Chinese Immigration.
By what means?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
By any means they
choose. Let them bring forward any evidence they can to substantiate their status, but we cannot continue to depend on these certificates of identity that were previously used. I had to send an officer all the way to China to take the matter up with the Chinese Government and the British authorities there, which has cost us a great deal of money and the conclusion we have come to, after going into the whole matter very fully, is, as I say, for the time being to abolish these certificates of identity. It is the only safe course to pursue.

At the same time I am sure my hon. friend would not stretch this regulation to such an extent as to bar those who, under the law or under the comity of nations, are admissable now. I

know that we must not encourage fake immigrants to come from that country to Canada, but if the matter is left entirely to the discretion of departmental officers I am afraid it might work injustice in some cases. I do not say it would, but it might. Is the matter left entirely to the discretion of the officers of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, not entirely as the section reads "who shall substantiate their status to the satisfaction of the controller subject to the approval of the minister." I doubt if there would be the slightest trouble with members of the diplomatic corps.

I know, as a matter of fact, that during the past two years, as my hon. friend says, in view of the laxity of Government control in Canton, passports and papers were signed by the hundreds and thousands not only for Canada but for the United States. Under those conditions I quite understand that the department is not willing to accept as bona fide documents such papers as have been presented within the period mentioned. On the other hand there are certain Chinese immigrants who, under the comity of nations, are entitled to be admitted into any country, such as merchants, clergymen and students. There are many Chinese students in the universities, and it should be easy for our officers to detect who is who.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is just where the trouble lies. For instance, in the first five months of last year from January to June we admitted forty-five merchants, but during the year we admitted no less than 1,309, who came with certificates of identity.
What about students?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We applied the student law a year ago. We got in about 2,000 in one year.
They were all students.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, and they came with certificates of identy.
There is always something to learn.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There will be no difficulty in regard to members ,of the diplomatic corps, Chinese clergymen, and similar men, but as regards the other class, until such time as there is stable government in China we feel that this is the only safe course to pursue to protect ourselves.

I am in sympathy with the object of the law, but I differ with my 
hon. friend as regards the indiscriminate stoppage of the student class. I believe in the Chinese student.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So do I, but we found most of them in the laundries.

I believe in the Chinese student because he will take back to his country some of the ideals of Canada and of the United States, which I think will work for the reformation of China. Does my hon. friend believe that so many students go into the laundry business or something of that kind. I am surprised that they should come for other purposes than entering our universities.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have no trouble with the student class now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister says he sent an officer to China. Have the members of the Chinese government approved of his method of proceeding?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would doubt that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The United States have had a good deal of trouble in dealing with immigration from China. Are the powers the minister is seeking under this legislation similar to the powers they have in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say, I have not examined the American law.
We are not legislating for the United States, but for Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I hear the
hon. member saying that we are not following the legislation of the United States.
I say we are not legislating for the United States but for Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly,
but we want to benefit by the experience of the United States. I should think one of the first steps the Government would take before drafting a Bill of this character would be to benefit by the experience of other countries. For that reason I ask the minister whether he has taken the trouble to find what methods the American Government are employing.
They are following the action of the minister in preventing an influx of students.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My impression was that this Bill based on the methods the United States had adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not looked into the matter at all, but I shall be very much interested to know the course they are following. My own impression is that outside of persons belonging to the diplomatic corps and other similar classes, the question whether Chinese immigrants shall enter the United States is determined by their officers, which is the way we are proposing here. Our difficulty at present is that the Justice Department has advised us that as our law entitles these people to enter Canada when they produce these certificates, we could not keep them out, no matter if we were certain they were misrepresenting their status. If the law were operationg properly, I should very much like to see the provision stand as in the, but we have had so much difficulty in the last two years that it seems the only course open to us is to change the law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think it is desirable-
Carried.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If my hon. friend wishes the Bill to be carried he will have to behave a little better than he is behaving at the moment. I think it is desirable in every way that Chinese immigration should be restricted, and that fraud should be prevented as far as possible, but any one who knows the Chinese will realize that they are very sensitive and very quick to appreciate courtesy. The American Government have been at great pains to avoid offending China in any way, and I think we should be equally careful. While I am most anxious that proper restrictions should be imposed, I should be sorry to see our Government placed in a position where any of these oriental people may feel that we are acting towards them more arbitrarily than our neighbours to the south. If the minister can give us an assurance that his action is not liable to be misconstrued, I think his measure is a perfectly safe and sound one.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will not take the Bill out of committee. I shall inquire how the American law is so we may know exactly what others are doing in this regard.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-definition of prohibited persons in Immigration Act made applicable to Chinese:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a difference in the two sections. We are simply making them the same.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-refund of tax on return within two years:

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should like to have the views of members, especially of those from British Columbia, in reference to this section. Under the present law if a Chinaman goes back tor China, and wishes to return to this country, he must obtain a certificate before leaving and if he returns within one year that certificate gives him the right to re-enter without again paying the head tax. It is proposed to extend that term to two years.
Does the minister mean that if a Chinamen goes back home he will get a refund of the head tax of $500?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. Under the law as it stands when he leaves Canada he gets a certificate from our department, which entitles him at any time within one year to return to Canada without again paying the head tax. Now it is proposed to extend that time from one year to two years.

A large number of
Chinese persons who come to Canada return to China for the accomplishment of certain rites in their native country. China is passing through a revolutionary period and that condition may continue for some years. As the Chinese who return to their own country may be detained on this account, or for family or other reasons, it seems to me that this extension of time is Christian in its character and I stand by it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-power to arrest prohibited persons:

What change is made by
this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The first change is to
make this law conform with the general Immigration Act in respect to the definition of prohibited persons. Under the law as it stands, if a person belongs to a prohibited class he may be either imprisoned or deported. We have cut out the imprisonment and made the person liable only to deportation. Then there is a provision that the question whether a person is liable to deportation shall be determined by the controller.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

Shall
I report the Bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the minister will give any required information

on the third reading, I have no desire to keep the Bill in committee. It can be recommitted if anything important comes up.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 138, to amend the Criminal Code, was read the second time.
On motion of Mr. Doherty that the House go into committee on the Bill:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is a
very long Bill, and I do not think that the minister ought to attempt to go further with it in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not suggest
that we take up anything about which there should be the slightest difference of opinion. There are a large number of clauses; I think quite a number would give rise to no discussion at all, and these we might deal with. It is not impossible that any that develop any very serious objection might be dropped altogether.

The question whether or
not a clause is continuous is a matter of opinion. The few members who are here might not think them contentious, but others who are not here might take a different view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will take the other man's opinion on that point, not my own.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think the minister will make as much progress with his Bill if he does not attempt to go on with it at this hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Very well.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
Progress reported.

subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. SPEAKER announced that he had received a message from His Excellency the Governor General. The message was read to the House as follows:
Devonshire.
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
I have received with great pleasure the Address that you have voted in reply to my Speech at the opening of Parliament and thank you for it sincerely.
On motion of Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 12.53 a.m. Tuesday.

Wednesday, May 25, 1921
